0.title: Do Not Be Shaken
0.overview:
Second Thessalonians was written from Corinth only weeks or months after the first letter — probably in the autumn of AD 51. Paul had received further news from Thessalonica, and it was concerning. Someone — perhaps a forged letter, perhaps a claimed prophecy — had convinced some in the congregation that 'the day of the Lord has already come' (2:2). The eschatological excitement of the first letter had curdled into eschatological anxiety, and in that anxiety some had stopped working altogether, apparently reasoning that if the day was upon them, there was no point in continuing with ordinary life.

Paul writes with unusual urgency to address both the false teaching and its practical consequences. His response to the doctrinal error is one of the most detailed accounts of events preceding the Second Coming in the New Testament — the rebellion, the man of lawlessness, the restrainer, the strong delusion. His response to the practical error is one of the most direct ethical instructions in all his letters: if anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat. The two problems are connected: a false eschatology produces disordered living; a true eschatology produces ordered, purposeful, patiently working discipleship.

Did Paul write this letter? Some scholars doubt it, because it is so like 1 Thessalonians in wording yet seems to speak differently about the end: there the day comes suddenly, here certain events must come first. But the letter was received as Paul’s from the earliest days, it closes with his own signature, This is the sign of genuineness in every letter of mine (3:17), and the two pictures fit together: the day will surprise the unprepared, yet God has set what must precede it. The more likely conclusion is that Paul wrote it, within months of the first letter, to correct a misunderstanding of it.

The letter is framed by two great convictions. The first is the righteous judgment of God (chapter 1): those who afflict the Thessalonians will face divine retribution; those who are afflicted will receive relief. The God who sees the suffering of his people does not leave it unanswered. The second is the faithfulness of God (chapter 3): 'The Lord is faithful. He will establish you and guard you against the evil one' (3:3). Between the sovereign judgment of the first chapter and the guarding faithfulness of the last runs the most extraordinary theological disclosure of the letter — the mystery of lawlessness, the restrainer, and the man of lawlessness whose coming precedes the Lord's. Paul does not explain everything; he explains enough to steady the congregation and call them back to the settled, working, praying life of those who know their God and wait for his Son.

1.title: Relief Is Coming
1.overview:
Within months of his first letter, Paul writes again. The persecution in Thessalonica has grown worse, someone is claiming (perhaps in Paul’s name) that the day of the Lord has already come, and some believers have stopped working. Chapter 1 steadies a suffering church before any correction comes.

Paul thanks God that their faith and love are growing under pressure, and says their endurance is itself evidence that God is at work. Then he answers the question suffering always raises: will wrong go unanswered? No. When the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven, God will give relief to the afflicted and justice against those who reject him, who will be shut out from his presence. On that day Christ will be glorified in his people. Paul prays that God will make them worthy of that calling, by his power and grace.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul, Silvanus and Timothy greet the Thessalonian church, again describing it as living in God the Father and the Lord Jesus, and wish them grace and peace.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why a Second Letter So Soon

Within months the Thessalonians were being told, possibly under Paul's own name, that the day of the Lord had already come (2:2), and the idleness the first letter warned about had hardened. Paul lays the foundation first: grace and peace from God our Father — and everything hard in the letter sits inside that frame (3:16, 18).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A church squeezed by hostility outside and a rumour inside is first told where it is: in God our Father.

Now: A frightened congregation cannot hear correction until it has been steadied, and the steadying is doctrinal rather than emotional.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, To the church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, To the church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

Meaning first. 2 Thessalonians was written a few months after the first letter, because the church faced worsening persecution, confusion about the day of the Lord, and continuing idleness among some members. Chapter 1 addresses the persecution. Paul thanks God that their faith and love are growing and boasts of their endurance (vv. 1–4). Their suffering is evidence of God’s just judgement: he will count them worthy of his kingdom, and repay their persecutors (vv. 5–6). This will happen when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his mighty angels in flaming fire, punishing those who do not know God or obey the gospel with eternal destruction away from his presence, and being glorified among his saints (vv. 7–10). So Paul prays that God will make them worthy of his calling and fulfil their every good purpose, so that Christ’s name is glorified in them (vv. 11–12). The chapter teaches the justice of God, the certainty of judgement, and the hope of the persecuted, and it ends with the most astonishing sentence in the letter: that the Lord of the flaming fire will be glorified in people like these, and they in him.

The setting. Written soon after 1 Thessalonians, probably also from Corinth around AD 51 (Acts 18:11). Something had gone badly wrong. Word had reached Paul that the Thessalonians were being told the day of the Lord had already come (2:2), and worse, that the claim was circulating under his own name, perhaps in a forged letter. The persecution had intensified. And the idleness he had warned about in the first letter had hardened into a real problem (3:6–12). He writes again within months.

Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy. The greeting is almost word for word what he wrote before, and the repetition is the point. The same three men: Paul; Silvanus, the Silas of Acts, who had been beaten and jailed with Paul at Philippi just before they reached Thessalonica (Acts 16:19–24; 17:1–4); and Timothy, whom Paul had sent back to strengthen them (1 Thessalonians 3:2). The same church. The same grace and peace. A congregation thrown into confusion is being told, before any argument begins, that nothing at the foundation has moved.

To the church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. One small change from the first letter repays catching. There he wrote in God the Father (1 Thessalonians 1:1); here it is in God our Father. It is a single word, and it gathers everybody in, Paul, Silvanus, Timothy and the harassed congregation in Macedonia, under one fatherhood. They are not a mission field being addressed by its founders. They are the same family. And the address makes a claim about location. Not in Thessalonica, where the pressure was; not in the confusion, which is where their minds were. In God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Paul tells them where they actually are before he tells them anything else, and he sets the Father and the Son side by side as the one sphere in which a church lives. No apostle would place a mere man beside God like that.

Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace is God’s undeserved favour, the whole of his kindness given to people who had earned the opposite; peace is what that favour produces: reconciliation with God, and the settled wholeness that flows from it. Both come equally from the Father and the Son, one source named twice. And both nouns are about to be tested. This letter contains flaming fire, eternal destruction, a man of lawlessness, a strong delusion, and a congregation instructed to withdraw from some of its own members. It opens with grace and peace, and it will close the same way (3:16, 18). Everything hard sits inside that frame.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church was at peace outwardly. They were persecuted, and they were confused. But God’s peace was theirs, and Paul’s greeting is not a pleasantry but a delivery: he is handing them, in the name of the Father and the Son, the thing their circumstances could not take away.

Why does Paul repeat almost exactly what he wrote before? Because frightened people need to hear that the ground has not shifted. Someone had told the Thessalonians that the end had come and they had missed it, and had used Paul’s name to say so (2:2). The quickest way to steady them was to sound exactly like himself: the same men, the same names for God, the same blessing. Repetition in Scripture is rarely filler. When God says the same thing twice, it is because his people need it twice, and Christians who have heard the gospel a thousand times still need the thousand-and-first.

In a sentence. From Paul, Silas and Timothy, to the church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: grace and peace to you from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

On a Tuesday. Whatever pressures you face, God’s grace and peace are yours today. When you are unsettled, by news, by a rumour in the church, by a voice that says everything has changed, go back to what has not changed: who your Father is, who your Lord is, and where you are. You are not chiefly in your workplace, your diagnosis or your argument. You are in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

For worship. Our Father does not change his greeting when his children are in trouble. He speaks the same grace and the same peace over the frightened church that he spoke over the flourishing one, because neither was ever based on how they were doing. The Father who gave his Son, and the Son who gave himself, stand together at the head of this letter as the one fountain of every blessing, and nothing in the fire or the confusion that follows will reach back far enough to dry it up.
verseByVerse.note: Written soon after 1 Thessalonians, probably also from Corinth, to a church still under persecution and now confused about the day of the Lord.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul says thanksgiving for them is a debt he owes God, because their faith is thriving and their love for one another is growing, and he holds up their perseverance under persecution as an example to other churches. Their suffering is a sign that God judges rightly and counts them fit for his kingdom. God will repay their persecutors and give his afflicted people rest when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his angels in flaming fire. Those who refuse to know God or obey the gospel will suffer everlasting ruin, cut off from the Lord’s presence and glory, on the day he comes to be honoured among his people. So Paul prays that God will make them worthy of their calling and by his power bring every good intention and work of faith to completion, so that Jesus is honoured in them and they in him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Judgment as Justice

Recompense is grounded in God's justice, not his temper (v.6), and ekdikesis is a just penalty imposed by the one authorised to impose it — which is why Christians may never take revenge (Rom 12:19). Verse 9's ‘eternal destruction’ has been read by conditionalists as final cessation and by the historic Reformed majority as unending ruin; both readings agree that its heart is exclusion ‘from the presence of the Lord’.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The promise of judgment was given to persecuted people not as a licence for revenge but as its removal: let God judge, and endure.

Now: This doctrine is written for patience, not satisfaction, by a man with unceasing anguish for those outside (Rom 9:2-3); and on that day the exhibit is the saints themselves (v.10).

verseByVerse.quote: We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers, as is right, because your faith is growing abundantly, and the love of every one of you for one another is increasing. Therefore we ourselves boast about you in the churches of God for your steadfastness and faith in all your persecutions and in the afflictions that you are enduring.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers, as is right, because your faith is growing abundantly, and the love of every one of you for one another is increasing. Therefore we ourselves boast about you in the churches of God for your steadfastness and faith in all your persecutions and in the afflictions that you are enduring.

We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers, as is right. That is a curious way to open a thanksgiving, and it is different from the first letter, where he simply gave thanks. Here he says he is under obligation to. The word is opheilomen: we owe it, as one owes a debt. Thanksgiving is a debt owed to God. Some have wondered whether the Thessalonians had protested at his earlier praise, thinking it too generous for people struggling as they were. Paul’s reply, if so, is that thanking God for them is not flattery he might turn down. It is a debt he has to pay, because of what God has visibly done. And notice to whom the thanks goes: not to the Thessalonians, but to God for them. Their growth is his work.

Because your faith is growing abundantly. What God has done is stated in two verbs that both strain upward. Their faith is growing abundantly: hyperauxanei, a compound found nowhere else in the New Testament, growing beyond, over-growing, the way a vine outruns its trellis. Paul had prayed for exactly this, that he might supply what was lacking in their faith (1 Thessalonians 3:10). God answered.

And the love of every one of you for one another is increasing. The second verb is pleonazei: overflowing, running past the brim. Paul had prayed for this too, that the Lord would make them increase and abound in love for one another (1 Thessalonians 3:12), and God answered that prayer as well. Stop on the detail in the middle: the love of every one of you. Not the love of the congregation in general, which is the sort of thing anyone can say about a church. Paul claims it of each person individually, with no exceptions, in a community under enough external pressure to make people brittle. Persecuted groups usually turn on each other. Fear makes people suspicious, and suffering makes them short. This one was not turning in; it was overflowing outward.

Therefore we ourselves boast about you in the churches of God. It is a startling thing for an apostle to admit. The pronoun is emphatic: we ourselves do it. Paul, who insisted to these very people that he never sought glory from anyone (1 Thessalonians 2:6), goes round the churches talking about them. He tells other congregations what God is doing in Thessalonica.

For your steadfastness and faith in all your persecutions and in the afflictions that you are enduring. See what he boasts of, because it is not their numbers or their gifts or their buildings. It is their steadfastness, hypomonē, the endurance that stays under a load without putting it down, and their faith, which here leans toward faithfulness: still trusting, still loyal. The participle is present: the afflictions are still going on as he writes. He is not circulating a success story about a church that came through. He is telling other congregations about people who are, at that moment, still under it and still standing. Persecution had not destroyed their faith; God had used it to strengthen it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean persecution is good. Persecution is the sin of those who inflict it, and Paul will say in v. 6 that God will repay it. It means God uses it to grow faith, the way a gardener uses the very wind that bends a young tree to drive its roots deeper.

Is it right to boast about a church? Doesn’t that feed pride? It depends on what is being boasted about and to whom the credit goes. Paul has just thanked God for this growth; his boasting is the public side of his thanksgiving, telling others what God has done (compare 1 Corinthians 1:31). He does not praise their talent but their endurance, which is the Spirit’s fruit. Boasting of that kind encourages weaker churches, honours God, and lets struggling believers know their faithfulness has been seen. What would be wrong is boasting in size, prestige or our own cleverness, or praising people in a way that hides the God behind them.

My faith doesn’t feel as if it is growing. What then? Growth is rarely visible from inside, and often seen first by others. The Thessalonians probably felt anything but strong; they were frightened and confused, and Paul still saw their faith over-growing. Measure growth not by feelings of strength but by what is still standing: you are still praying, still coming back to Christ, still loving people who are hard to love, still holding on under pressure you did not choose. That holding is growth. And ask God for it, as Paul did for them, because it is his gift before it is your achievement.

In a sentence. We ought always to thank God for you, brothers and sisters, and rightly so, because your faith is growing more and more, and the love all of you have for one another is increasing. Therefore, among God’s churches we boast about your perseverance and faith in all the persecutions and trials you are enduring.

On a Tuesday. Think of one believer you know who is under pressure and still standing: an illness, a hostile workplace, a hard marriage, a family that mocks their faith. Thank God for them by name today, and then tell them what you see. Paul did not keep his admiration for the Thessalonians private; he let them know that others knew. A single sentence from you may be the evidence someone needs that their endurance is not invisible. And pray for persecuted churches you will never visit, whose steadfastness is still being boasted about in heaven.

For worship. The same God who answered Paul’s prayers for Thessalonica is answering prayers now in churches whose names we do not know: faith over-growing in prison cells, love overflowing in villages where believers are beaten for gathering. He takes frightened, ordinary people and makes them stand, and then he makes them love one another under the very pressure meant to break them apart. Their steadfastness is his workmanship, and every word of thanks for it is a debt owed to him and gladly paid.

verseByVerse.quote: This is evidence of the righteous judgment of God, that you may be considered worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you are also suffering—
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is evidence of the righteous judgment of God, that you may be considered worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you are also suffering—

This is evidence of the righteous judgment of God. Now Paul says something about their suffering that is easy to misread, so it needs taking slowly. What is evidence? Not the persecution itself: God is not vindicated by the fact that his people are being hurt. The nearest antecedent is what he has just described, their steadfastness and faith under it. Their endurance is the exhibit. The word endeigma is a legal term for evidence produced in court, proof, sign, and Paul is saying that a group of ordinary people holding their ground under sustained hostility is a fact requiring explanation, and the explanation is that God is at work. He is at work in them, preparing them, and he will vindicate them. It is the same logic he used with the Philippians, whose fearlessness he called a clear sign of their salvation, and that from God (Philippians 1:28). Nobody stands like that over nothing.

That you may be considered worthy of the kingdom of God. “Considered worthy” (kataxiōthēnai) means counted worthy, judged fit. Worthiness here is not merit earned by suffering; that would contradict everything Paul teaches, and he will pray later in the chapter that God would make them worthy (v. 11), which he would not need to do if they were achieving it themselves. It is fittedness. God, by grace, counts them worthy, and their endurance shows the genuineness of their faith. The kingdom they are heading for is one where God is King and everything false has been dealt with, and people are being shaped now for living there.

For which you are also suffering. They suffer because they belong to God’s kingdom. Paul had told new converts in Galatia that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God (Acts 14:22), and he had warned the Thessalonians in person that they were destined for affliction (1 Thessalonians 3:3–4). Their affliction is not random misfortune that God is making the best of. It is specifically because of the kingdom: they are suffering for the thing they are being fitted for. That is a different sentence from God will bring good out of this, and a stronger one. Suffering for the kingdom is a mark of belonging to it.

The weight of it. The pastoral force of the verse is considerable for anyone paying a price. Paul does not tell them their suffering is meaningless and will simply be compensated later. He tells them it is doing something now, and that their capacity to bear it is itself the proof that God has not looked away. The world reads their pain as evidence that their God is weak or absent. Paul reads it the other way round. A God who was absent would have left them to collapse. They have not collapsed.

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation is earned by suffering. It is by grace. But those saved by grace endure, and their endurance is evidence.

What about suffering that has nothing to do with my faith, like illness or grief? This verse speaks specifically of suffering for the kingdom: hostility because you belong to Christ. But the wider truth reaches further. Scripture teaches that God works all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28), and that every trial a believer endures is used by the Father to refine and train (Hebrews 12:5–11; 1 Peter 1:6–7). Your illness is not persecution, and you need not call it that. But the endurance God gives you in it is still his work, still evidence of grace, and still preparing you for the kingdom where there will be no more pain.

In a sentence. All this is evidence that God’s judgement is right, and as a result you will be counted worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you are suffering.

On a Tuesday. If you suffer for Christ, see it as evidence that you belong to his kingdom. The colleague who freezes you out because you will not join the joke, the relative who sneers at your faith, the promotion that went elsewhere because you would not shade the truth: none of it is a sign that God has forgotten you. It is the old mark of citizenship. Do not go looking for suffering, and do not dramatise ordinary friction. But when it comes because of Christ, do not be ashamed. Thank him that you are counted among those who bear his name.

For worship. The righteous Judge is not waiting until the last day to begin his work. He is already at work in the hidden places where his people are under pressure, holding them up, fitting them for glory, writing his evidence into their endurance. The kingdom they suffer for is the kingdom he is preparing them for, and the King of it walked this road first: he suffered for the kingdom before any of his people did, and through his suffering opened the door they will walk through.

verseByVerse.quote: since indeed God considers it just to repay with affliction those who afflict you, and to grant relief to you who are afflicted as well as to us, when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his mighty angels
verseByVerse.commentary:
since indeed God considers it just to repay with affliction those who afflict you, and to grant relief to you who are afflicted as well as to us, when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his mighty angels

Since indeed God considers it just to repay with affliction those who afflict you. Paul grounds what follows not in God’s anger but in his justice. The word is the righteousness word: this is what a fair verdict looks like. That distinction matters, because divine judgement is often imagined as a loss of temper. It is the opposite. A judge who let cruelty pass without response would not be merciful; he would be unjust, and we would say so about any human court. The people afflicting the Thessalonians had made choices, and those choices had victims. Paul says there will be an accounting, and that the accounting is the work of a good God rather than a provoked one. God’s justice requires that persecutors be repaid. Not personal revenge, which Christians are forbidden (Romans 12:19), but God’s right judgement.

And to grant relief to you who are afflicted as well as to us. The symmetry is exact and deliberate: affliction repaid to the afflicters, and to the afflicted, relief. The word is anesis: a loosening, a slackening of tension, rest, release. It is what happens when a strained rope is let out, or a besieged city is relieved. These people had been under pressure for months with no let-up. Paul promises not merely compensation but release. And note the words he adds: as well as to us. Paul puts himself on the same side of the ledger. He is not an official announcing an outcome from a safe distance; he is another man waiting for the same rest.

When the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven. Then the verse turns, and the timing is everything: relief comes when the Lord Jesus is revealed. Not before. Paul does not promise the persecution will stop, and it did not. What he gives them is a date they cannot see and cannot hurry, which is a harder comfort than deliverance next month and a far more durable one. “Revealed” is apokalypsis: an unveiling, the drawing back of a curtain on something that was there all along. That is the governing idea of the whole passage. Now hidden from sight, Christ will be unveiled publicly at his return. Nothing is being created on that day; something is being shown. The Lord these people already serve, and the justice they cannot presently see, will simply become visible.

With his mighty angels. Literally, the angels of his power. They accompany him as his army and his servants (Matthew 13:41; 25:31). Notice whose angels they are: his. The one who was arrested in a garden, and who said he could have called on more than twelve legions of angels and did not (Matthew 26:53), returns with them at his command.

One coming, not two. Notice what happens at this one unveiling: relief for the afflicted church and judgement on its afflicters, together, on the same day, in public, from heaven. Paul knows of no earlier, secret coming in which believers are quietly removed before the trouble. Their rest begins at the same visible revelation at which the persecutors are repaid. That is why the app reads the Lord’s return as a single, glorious, public event at the end of the age, bringing the resurrection, the gathering of the saints and the final judgement together (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; Matthew 25:31–32). The hope of the church is not escape from the world’s last troubles but the appearing of its King.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers should seek revenge. They leave it to God, and precisely because they can leave it to him, they are freed to bless those who curse them (Romans 12:14, 19–21).

Is it wrong to want God to punish those who have hurt me? Wanting justice is not wrong: the souls under the altar cry out for it (Revelation 6:10), and the psalms are full of the cry. What is wrong is wanting to take it yourself, or wanting the person to be lost rather than repent. A Christian holds both: a real longing for wrong to be put right, handed over to God, and a real prayer that the one who did it might be converted, as Saul the persecutor was. Paul himself was once on the other side of this verse. Leave the verdict to the Judge, and pray for the defendant.

Why does God let persecution go on so long? Because his patience is giving time for repentance, including the repentance of persecutors (2 Peter 3:9), and because he is doing something in his suffering people that comfort could not do (v. 5). The delay is not neglect. The Thessalonians did not see the end in their lifetimes, and their persecutors may have died unrepaid by any human court. But the date is fixed, and no case is closed until the Judge closes it.

In a sentence. God is just: he will pay back trouble to those who trouble you and give relief to you who are troubled, and to us as well. This will happen when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven in blazing fire with his powerful angels.

On a Tuesday. If you have been wronged for your faith, entrust it to God. Write down, if it helps, what was done to you, and then pray it over to him: this is yours, Lord, not mine. Then do the next kind thing for the person, because you no longer have to make sure they pay. The believer who knows God is just is the only person who can afford to be gentle.

For worship. The Lord Jesus is not absent; he is hidden, and the day of his unveiling is already on the calendar of heaven. The one who was mocked by soldiers will be revealed with the armies of heaven at his command. The one who was afflicted for us will give rest to all who are afflicted for him. No tear of his people is lost, no cruelty forgotten, and when the curtain is drawn back the whole creation will see that the King was on his throne all along, just in every judgement and kind in every delay.

verseByVerse.quote: in flaming fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and on those who do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
in flaming fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and on those who do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus.

In flaming fire. Fire is the standing Old Testament image for God made visible and for his holy judgement: the bush that burned and was not consumed (Exodus 3:2), the pillar that went before Israel, the mountain at Sinai wrapped in smoke because the LORD had descended on it in fire (Exodus 19:18), the LORD who will come in fire to render his anger (Isaiah 66:15), and the Ancient of Days whose throne was fiery flames (Daniel 7:9–10). Paul is not inventing a new picture; he is putting Jesus where the God of Sinai stood. That is how the earliest Christians spoke about the carpenter from Nazareth.

Inflicting vengeance. “Vengeance” is a word modern readers wince at, and the wince repays examining. It translates ekdikēsis: just punishment, justice carried out. It is not personal spite. Paul forbids personal revenge flatly (Romans 12:19), quoting the Lord’s word that vengeance is his, and that is exactly the point: it belongs to God, not to us. Ekdikēsis is the imposing of a just penalty by the one authorised to impose it, and here Christ himself carries it out. The whole reason a Christian can be told never to take revenge is that God has undertaken to see the matter dealt with.

On those who do not know God. Paul names who this falls on, in two phrases, and the pairing is deliberate. The first is Old Testament language for the pagan world, the nations that do not know God (Psalm 79:6; Jeremiah 10:25). These are not people who never had any light. Paul taught that what can be known about God is plain to everyone, and that people suppress it (Romans 1:18–21, 28). Not knowing God, in Scripture, is not innocent ignorance but a refusal of the knowledge that was available.

And on those who do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus. The second phrase describes people who have heard the message and refused it. Between them the two phrases cover everyone, the uninformed and the informed, and Paul lets them stand together under one verdict. And do not miss the verb attached to the gospel: not those who do not believe it but those who do not obey it. That is a striking way to speak of good news, and Paul uses it more than once (Romans 10:16). The gospel is not merely an offer to be considered on its merits. It is the announcement that God has installed his Son as King, and it comes with a command: God commands all people everywhere to repent (Acts 17:30). To shrug at it is not neutrality; it is a refusal.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God judges people for what they could not know. Everyone has rejected some light from God, and each is judged by the light he was given (Romans 2:12).

What about people who have never heard the gospel? They are not judged for rejecting a gospel they never heard; they are judged for refusing the God they did know, in creation and conscience (Romans 1:20; 2:14–16). But the Bible gives no hope that anyone is saved apart from Christ: there is salvation in no one else (Acts 4:12), and people call on him only when they hear (Romans 10:13–15). That is why this verse should send the church to the nations, not into speculation. We leave the hidden judgements to a God who is perfectly just, and we do what he commanded: go and tell.

What does it mean to obey the gospel? It means to do what the gospel calls for: to repent of sin and trust Jesus Christ as Saviour and Lord. Obedience here is not earning salvation by good works; it is the obedience of faith (Romans 1:5), bowing to the King by receiving him. From that first obedience flows a life of following him, imperfectly and truly. The person who believes the gospel obeys it; the person who refuses to come has disobeyed it, however politely.

In a sentence. He will punish those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Obey the gospel today: trust and follow Christ. If you have been keeping him at arm’s length, considering him, admiring him, postponing him, recognise that as disobedience to a King, and come. And pray for those who do not know God, by name. Then ask whether one of them has ever heard the gospel from you clearly enough to obey it.

For worship. The fire of Sinai now burns around the Lord Jesus, and it is his right. He is the God who came down on the mountain, and the God who came down in the manger, and he will come again in flaming fire as the rightful King of all the earth. Yet the same Lord who will command the fire once stood under it in our place, so that everyone who obeys the gospel finds that the fire has already fallen on him, and has nothing left to burn.

verseByVerse.quote: They will suffer the punishment of eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his might,
verseByVerse.commentary:
They will suffer the punishment of eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his might,

They will suffer the punishment. “Punishment” (dikē) means penalty, justice: what is due. This is among the most solemn sentences Paul wrote, and it should be handled carefully and without relish.

Of eternal destruction. “Eternal” (aiōnios) is the word used for eternal life: the age-to-come word, everlasting. Jesus sets eternal punishment and eternal life side by side in one sentence (Matthew 25:46). “Destruction” (olethros) means ruin, undoing, the loss of everything good. It does not by itself mean annihilation. Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians 5:5 of a man handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, and that man goes on existing and is expected to be restored. The ruin is a state, and the word eternal tells us it is never reversed.

Away from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his might. This is the clause to weigh. “Presence” is literally face, and the phrase echoes Isaiah 2, where men hide from before the terror of the LORD and from the splendour of his majesty. Whatever else the sentence describes, it defines the punishment as an exclusion, a being-put-outside: shut out from the face of God, the source of all joy, light and life (Matthew 7:23; 25:41). Hell is not most deeply a chamber of torments but an absence: the loss of the presence of the God who is the source of every good thing anyone has ever enjoyed, including those who never acknowledged where it came from. Every kindness, every beauty, every ordinary pleasure of a human life came from him. To be finally away from him is to be away from all of it. Separated from his favour, though not from his justice: God is present in hell in his holiness, and absent in every blessing.

Where Christians differ: eternal punishment or annihilation? Some (annihilationists or conditionalists, among them Edward Fudge, Clark Pinnock and, tentatively, John Stott) argue that eternal destruction means the wicked cease to exist, a destruction whose results are eternal. Universalists say all will eventually be saved. Verdict: Eternal destruction is everlasting, conscious ruin: exclusion from God’s gracious presence forever. The same word “eternal” describes both the punishment of the wicked and the life of the righteous (Matthew 25:46). Scripture speaks of the smoke of their torment rising forever and ever (Revelation 14:11; 20:10), and of unquenchable fire (Mark 9:43–48). This is the historic Christian teaching (Westminster 33.2). It is terrible, and should move believers to tears and to urgent evangelism, as it moved Paul (Romans 9:2–3).

How a Christian holds this. Two things should be said. First, Paul is not writing to gratify anyone’s appetite for the fate of their enemies. He is writing to people being hurt, to tell them that the wrong will not stand forever, and the effect he intends is patience, not satisfaction. Second, this is written by a man who elsewhere says he has great sorrow and unceasing anguish in his heart for those outside, and could wish himself accursed for their sake (Romans 9:2–3). Anyone who can state this doctrine without grief has not understood it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God delights in punishment: he has no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live (Ezekiel 33:11). It means he is just, and sin against an infinitely holy God is infinitely serious.

How can a God of love do this? Because love that is not also just is not love but indifference. A God who shrugged at cruelty, at the murder of children, at the oppression of the poor, at the contempt of his own Son, would not be kinder than the God of the Bible; he would be morally smaller. Hell is God giving people, finally and justly, what they chose: life without him. And the measure of his love is not that there is no judgement, but that he sent his Son to bear it for all who would come (Romans 5:8). No one is in hell who wanted God.

How can I be happy in heaven if someone I love is lost? This is one of the hardest questions a Christian asks, and Scripture does not give every detail. What it promises is that God will wipe away every tear (Revelation 21:4), and that on that day we will see his justice as clearly as his mercy, and will not find him wrong in anything. We will love what he loves, and agree with him completely. For now, the question should not paralyse you but propel you: while they live, the door is open. Pray for them, speak to them, and leave in God’s hands what only he can judge.

In a sentence. They will be punished with everlasting destruction and shut out from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his might.

On a Tuesday. Let this verse do what Paul meant it to do. If you are wronged, let it give you patience: the Judge will settle it. If you are careless, let it wake you: this is what it is to be without Christ. And if you know someone who is drifting from God, let it give you courage to speak, kindly and soon. Nobody who believes this verse can stay comfortable about the people next door.

For worship. The punishment of eternal destruction is what sinners deserve, and it is what the Son of God endured in his soul on the cross when he cried out, forsaken by his Father, so that those who trust him would never hear that cry from their own lips. He went outside the presence that he might bring us in. Thank Christ that he bore the punishment you deserved, and marvel that the face from which the lost are banished is the face that turned toward you in mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: when he comes on that day to be glorified in his saints, and to be marveled at among all who have believed, because our testimony to you was believed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
when he comes on that day to be glorified in his saints, and to be marveled at among all who have believed, because our testimony to you was believed.

When he comes on that day. The day of the Lord, the single day of his appearing. And the same sentence that describes the ruin of some describes the day as the moment Jesus comes to be glorified in his saints and marvelled at among all who have believed.

To be glorified in his saints. The preposition is the whole point. He is glorified in them, not merely by them. Not a crowd applauding from the edges while the glory happens elsewhere. His glory will be seen in the people he rescued, in what he has made of them, as what he has made reflects the one who made it. The exhibit on that day is the saints themselves. Think about who Paul is saying this to. A small, harassed congregation in a provincial city, meeting in somebody’s house, despised by their neighbours, with several of their number recently buried (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Paul tells them that when the Lord Jesus is revealed in flaming fire with his mighty angels, what everyone will be looking at is them, and in them, him.

And to be marveled at among all who have believed. “Marvelled at” is a strong verb: to be wondered at, to cause astonishment. Believers will marvel at him, overwhelmed with wonder, and the angels and the watching universe will marvel too. The language echoes the psalms, where God is greatly feared in the council of the holy ones (Psalm 89:7) and awesome from his sanctuary (Psalm 68:35). And the wonder is not at the saints’ achievement. It is at what grace did with such material. If you have ever thought your own case too far gone or too ordinary to be worth much, this verse says the finished work will be a thing that stops heaven in its tracks.

Because our testimony to you was believed. The final clause is easy to skip, and it is the hinge that connects the cosmic scene to a particular week in Thessalonica. Why will these people be among those in whom Christ is glorified? Because not much more than a year earlier three travelling men said something in their town and they believed it. The Thessalonians will be among them, a personal assurance. The whole blazing revelation, angels, fire, glory, the settling of every account, reaches these people through a testimony that was spoken and received. Paul will ask them in the next chapter to hold to what they were taught (2:15), and this is why. The last day runs through the ordinary act of believing what was said to you.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers will be glorified apart from Christ. His glory is reflected in them. They are the mirror, not the light.

Who are the saints? All who have believed. Paul puts the two phrases side by side: his saints, and all who have believed. Saint means holy one, someone set apart for God, and in the New Testament it is the ordinary name for every Christian (1 Corinthians 1:2). It is not a rank achieved by a few extraordinary people or conferred after death. If you trust Christ, you are one of the saints in whom he will be glorified, not because you are impressive but because he is.

In a sentence. On the day he comes to be glorified in his holy people and to be marvelled at among all those who have believed. This includes you, because you believed our testimony to you.

On a Tuesday. Look at the most unremarkable believer in your church, perhaps the one you find hardest to love, and then look in the mirror. Both of you are going to be part of the display of Christ’s glory on the last day. Treat one another accordingly. And when you are tempted to think your faith is too small to matter, remember the hinge: you believed the testimony. That is all the Thessalonians did, and it put them in the centre of the last day.

For worship. One day you will marvel at Christ, and so will every angel in heaven, and the cause of their wonder will be what he did with sinners like you. He will not be glorified in spite of his people, nor beside them, but in them: the rescued, the remade, the once-dead now shining with a light that is entirely his. Begin to marvel at him now. The astonishment of that day is only the eyes of faith opened wide.

verseByVerse.quote: To this end we always pray for you, that our God may make you worthy of his calling and may fulfill every resolve for good and every work of faith by his power, so that the name of our Lord Jesus may be glorified in you, and you in him, according to the grace of our God and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To this end we always pray for you, that our God may make you worthy of his calling and may fulfill every resolve for good and every work of faith by his power, so that the name of our Lord Jesus may be glorified in you, and you in him, according to the grace of our God and the Lord Jesus Christ.

To this end we always pray for you. With that day in view. Having described the day, Paul prays toward it. Everything in these two verses is aimed at the scene he has just painted. The coming of Christ is not, for Paul, a subject for charts; it is a reason to pray.

That our God may make you worthy of his calling. “Make worthy” (axiōsē) means count worthy, deem fit. And this petition answers a question v. 5 raised. There he said their suffering was shaping them to be considered worthy of the kingdom; someone might reasonably ask whether the worthiness is therefore their own achievement. Paul settles it: he prays that our God may make them worthy. It is something asked for, not earned. The endurance he praised in v. 4 he now requests from God in v. 11. God called them; may he make them live up to it (Ephesians 4:1). The calling is God’s effectual summons, by which he drew them to Christ through the gospel (2:14), and the God who called is the God who completes.

And may fulfill every resolve for good. Two things he asks God to bring to completion. The first is every resolve for good: the inward decision, the good intention formed, every desire for goodness God has planted in them. It is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:13).

And every work of faith by his power. The second is every work of faith: the thing actually done, every action springing from faith (1 Thessalonians 1:3). Paul knows how often the first dies before it reaches the second, the resolve made on Sunday and gone by Wednesday, and he asks God to carry both through. And he says how it happens: by his power. Not by their determination.

So that the name of our Lord Jesus may be glorified in you, and you in him. Verse 12 gives the purpose, and it is a two-way sentence that repays reading slowly. His name means his person and reputation, all that he is. The first half we might have expected: the aim of Christian living is his honour, seen in his people, which is exactly v. 10. The second half is astonishing and Paul does not pause over it. And you in him. The traffic runs both ways. He is glorified in them; they are glorified in him. Whatever glory they receive is not a separate award handed out alongside his; it is his own, shared with the people joined to him.

According to the grace of our God and the Lord Jesus Christ. The last clause keeps the whole thing where the letter began. Not according to their endurance, which has been considerable and which Paul has boasted about across several provinces. According to grace. All by grace, from beginning to end. The measure of what they receive is set by the giver’s generosity, not by the quality of their standing under pressure. Some read the phrase as our God and Lord, Jesus Christ, calling Jesus God directly; the Greek can be taken either way. Either way, grace comes from both, and Paul could only write the Father and the Son under one article of grace because the Son shares the Father’s deity.

What it does not mean. It does not mean worthiness is earned. God makes us worthy by grace.

If God does it all by his power, what do I do? You do the resolving and the working; God gives the power to do them. Paul prays for their resolve for good and their work of faith; both are really theirs. Grace does not make us passive; it makes us able. So you form good intentions and act on them, and you pray as you do, because the gap between Sunday’s resolution and Wednesday’s action is exactly where you need him. When a good desire stirs in you, to forgive, to give, to speak to a neighbour about Christ, treat it as something God may be starting, ask him to finish it, and take the first step today.

In a sentence. With this in mind, we constantly pray for you, that our God may make you worthy of his calling, and that by his power he may bring to fruition your every desire for goodness and your every deed prompted by faith. We pray this so that the name of our Lord Jesus may be glorified in you, and you in him, according to the grace of our God and the Lord Jesus Christ.

On a Tuesday. Pray this prayer for yourself and someone you love: that God would make you worthy of his calling, and fulfil every good desire and work of faith by his power. Name one good resolve you made recently and have not carried out. Bring it to God now, ask him to complete it, and do the first concrete part of it before the day ends.

For worship. The God who called us will not leave his calling half-done. He plants the good desire, he gives the power to act on it, and he brings the work to completion, all so that his Son may be glorified in his people. And then, astonishingly, he shares the glory: we are glorified in Christ, wearing a splendour that is entirely his and freely given. From the first grace of the greeting to the last grace of this prayer, everything is from our God and the Lord Jesus Christ, and everything returns to him in praise.
