2.title: The Mystery of Lawlessness
2.overview:
Someone had told the Thessalonians, perhaps by a forged letter in Paul’s name, that the day of the Lord had already come. To a persecuted church promised relief on that day (1:7), this was devastating: either the promise had failed, or they had been passed over. Paul answers with an argument they can check: the day cannot have come, because two things must happen first, the great rebellion and the revealing of the “man of lawlessness”, who sets himself up in God’s place. Something now restrains him; when it is removed he will appear, deceive those who refused to love the truth, and be destroyed by the Lord Jesus with a breath.

Paul had taught this in person (v. 5), so he writes in shorthand, and some details (above all the restrainer) are now uncertain. The pastoral point is plain: the worst coming evil is held back now, runs on God’s timetable, and ends effortlessly at Christ’s coming. So Paul turns to thanks: God chose them, the Spirit sanctifies them, and glory awaits. Stand firm and hold to what you were taught.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Some had alarmed the church by claiming, perhaps in a letter falsely attributed to Paul, that the day of the Lord had already come. Paul tells them not to be shaken. That day will not come before a great rebellion and the appearance of the man of lawlessness, who will oppose God, exalt himself above every object of worship and claim to be God. Something is restraining him for now, until it is removed. Then he will be revealed, and the Lord Jesus will destroy him by the breath of his mouth and the splendour of his coming. His arrival will be Satan’s work, with false signs and wonders that deceive those who are perishing because they refused to love the truth, so God gives them over to the lie they preferred.
verseByVerse.theology:
Judicial Hardening

God sends the delusion of verse 11 ‘therefore’ — because they refused to love the truth (v.10). It is a judicial response to a prior refusal, and it locates the failure in the affections, not the intellect: which is also why signs and wonders prove nothing on their own.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The claim that the day had already come was devastating to a persecuted church promised relief on that day (1:7); and Paul's language is allusive because he had taught them this in person (v.5).

Now: Paul gives a pattern to recognise, not a name to guess — and the six verses of build-up end with the Lord undoing the lawless one with a breath (v.8). The proportions are the message.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our being gathered together to him, we ask you, brothers, not to be quickly shaken in mind or alarmed, either by a spirit or a spoken word, or a letter seeming to be from us, to the effect that the day of the Lord has come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our being gathered together to him, we ask you, brothers, not to be quickly shaken in mind or alarmed, either by a spirit or a spoken word, or a letter seeming to be from us, to the effect that the day of the Lord has come.

Meaning first. 2 Thessalonians 2 corrects a false teaching that the day of the Lord had already come. Some in Thessalonica were alarmed, perhaps thinking they had missed Christ’s return, or that the persecution they suffered was the final judgement. Paul says: do not be shaken. That day will not come until two things happen first: the rebellion, a great falling away from God, and the revealing of the man of lawlessness, who will exalt himself above every god and claim to be God. Something is now restraining him, though the mystery of lawlessness is already at work. When he is revealed, the Lord Jesus will destroy him by the breath of his mouth and the splendour of his coming. His coming will be accompanied by Satanic power and false wonders, deceiving those who refused to love the truth; God will even send them a strong delusion (vv. 1–12). By contrast, Paul thanks God for the Thessalonians, chosen for salvation, called through the gospel to share Christ’s glory. So stand firm, hold to the apostolic teaching, and may God comfort and strengthen you (vv. 13–17). The darkest chapter in the letter is written to make frightened people calm, and it does so by showing them that even the last rebellion runs on God’s timetable and ends with a single breath from Christ.

Now concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. Here is the emergency that produced the letter, and both phrases in the verse point straight back to the first letter. “Coming” is parousia: arrival, presence, the word used in the ancient world for the state visit of a king to a city. It is the coming of 1 Thessalonians 4:15. Paul is picking up exactly where he left off, because that is the teaching that had been twisted.

And our being gathered together to him. “Gathered together” (episynagōgē) is precisely the scene of 1 Thessalonians 4:17: the dead raised and the living caught up to meet him in the air. It is the gathering of the elect from the four winds that Jesus promised at his coming (Matthew 24:31). Paul ties the two phrases together under one article: the coming and the gathering are one event, not two. The Lord comes, and his people are gathered to him.

We ask you, brothers, not to be quickly shaken in mind or alarmed. The first verb is saleuthēnai, used of a ship torn from its moorings and of an earthquake shaking a building: tossed like a ship at sea. The second, throeisthai, is a continuous present: not a single fright but an ongoing state of panic. Knocked off your foundations, and then kept rattled. That is a precise description of what false teaching about the end does to a church: it produces fear and instability. Notice too the word quickly. Paul is not surprised that a lie was told; he is grieved at how fast they let it move them.

Either by a spirit or a spoken word, or a letter seeming to be from us. Paul lists three possible channels for the claim, which is remarkable in itself. A spirit: a claimed prophecy, an utterance in the meeting. A spoken word: a sermon, teaching, or report. A letter: perhaps forged in Paul’s name. He does not know which it was, and the vagueness is genuine, but he takes seriously that any of the three could be the vehicle. Sit with the third. Someone had, or might have, written a letter pretending to be Paul in order to unsettle this congregation. That is why he signs this one in his own hand at the end and calls it the sign of genuineness in every letter of his (3:17). The apostolic mail was already being counterfeited within twenty-odd years of the resurrection.

To the effect that the day of the Lord has come. What the message claimed is the crux. The verb is enestēken, a perfect: it has arrived and is now present. Not that it is near, which is what Paul himself taught, but that it is here already and they had somehow missed it. Perhaps the teachers said it had begun spiritually, or that the judgements had started and the persecution was the proof. Now see why that was devastating rather than merely mistaken. These people were being persecuted. They had been promised relief when the Lord was revealed (1:7). If the day had already come and this was it, still hunted, still burying friends, no vindication, then either the promise had failed or they had been passed over. Every hope in the first letter collapses. No wonder they were shaken.

Does this rule out a secret rapture before the tribulation? Pretribulational Christians hold that the church will be taken away before the day of the Lord begins, and that the man of lawlessness will appear only after it has gone. But Paul treats the coming, the gathering and the day as one event, and he tells the Thessalonians that day will not come until the rebellion and the man of lawlessness appear (v. 3), which only makes sense if they will still be here to see them. If a secret removal were the next thing on the calendar, this was the moment to say so, and it would have been the simplest comfort in the world. He says nothing of the kind. The more likely reading is that there is one public return of Christ, at which he gathers his people and judges the lawless one (v. 8). Christians who hold the other view are our brothers, and we can hold this charitably; but the church should not expect to be spared the last troubles. It should expect to be kept through them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the second coming is unimportant. It means false claims about it must be rejected. Paul does not cure the panic by telling them to stop thinking about the Lord’s return; he cures it by teaching them about it properly.

How should I respond to end-times predictions today? With calm and with your Bible. Paul’s remedy for the Thessalonians was not a newer, better prediction but a return to what they had been taught. When someone announces that recent events prove the end is upon us, or names a date, or claims a special revelation about the timetable, ask the questions Paul would ask: does Scripture say this, or only the speaker? Does it make me more faithful, or only more anxious? Jesus said no one knows the day or hour (Matthew 24:36), and every date ever set has been wrong. Be ready every day, and unsettled by no one.

In a sentence. Concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our being gathered to him, we ask you, brothers and sisters, not to become easily unsettled or alarmed by the teaching allegedly from us, whether by a prophecy or by word of mouth or by letter, asserting that the day of the Lord has already come.

On a Tuesday. Do not be shaken by sensational claims about the end times. Test them by Scripture. Notice what you have been reading or watching about the future, and what it has done to you. If it has left you agitated, fascinated or fearful rather than steady, prayerful and kind, it has not been doing what Paul’s teaching does. Turn it off, and read 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18 and this chapter slowly instead.

For worship. The coming of our Lord Jesus Christ is not a rumour that can be counterfeited or a date that can slip by unnoticed. When the King comes, no one will need to be told; and when he gathers his people, not one of them will be missing. He is the Lord who holds history steady while men try to shake it, and his promise to come for his own has never once been in danger. The day has not passed us by. He is still coming, and he will come for us.
verseByVerse.note: Someone was claiming — perhaps even by a forged letter — that the day of the Lord had already come.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one deceive you in any way. For that day will not come, unless the rebellion comes first, and the man of lawlessness is revealed, the son of destruction,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let no one deceive you in any way. For that day will not come, unless the rebellion comes first, and the man of lawlessness is revealed, the son of destruction,

Let no one deceive you in any way. Blunt, and the phrase covers the lot: whatever the channel, whatever the credentials. Deception about the end is a real danger, and Jesus warned of it more than of anything else in his teaching on the last things: see that no one leads you astray, for many will come in my name (Matthew 24:4–5, 11, 24).

For that day will not come, unless the rebellion comes first. Now Paul’s argument, and its shape matters as much as its content. He does not reason from feelings or from the character of God. He gives them a checkable fact: certain things must happen first, and they plainly have not. Therefore the day has not come. It is an argument any of them could run without him, which is exactly what a frightened church needs. The first event is the rebellion: hē apostasia, with the article, the apostasy, a specific and expected event. The word means defection, falling away, revolt, and the Greek Old Testament uses it of turning away from God. A great rebellion against God, perhaps including widespread falling away from the faith in the professing church (Matthew 24:10–12; 1 Timothy 4:1; 2 Timothy 3:1–5). Paul assumes they know what he means, because he had told them (v. 5).

Which reading of the rebellion is most likely? The rebellion is most likely a great falling away from the faith within the professing church, as Jesus foretold, when the love of many will grow cold (Matthew 24:10–12), and as Paul warns elsewhere: in later times some will depart from the faith (1 Timothy 4:1). It may be joined to an open revolt of the world against God, but its heart is defection by those who once professed to belong. It is the climax of a defection already at work (v. 7).

And the man of lawlessness is revealed. Note the verb: revealed, apokalyphthē, the same word used of Christ’s own appearing in 1:7. Paul uses it three times of this figure in this passage. It is a deliberate and chilling parody: a counter-unveiling, a dark mirror of the real one. “Lawlessness” (anomia) is the rejection of God’s law. The phrase names his essence: not merely someone who breaks laws, but one whose principle is the abolition of God’s law and of any authority above himself. A figure of supreme rebellion against God. John calls him the antichrist (1 John 2:18). Some manuscripts read man of sin, as the ESV notes; the meaning is the same.

The son of destruction. A Hebrew idiom: one destined for destruction, who belongs to ruin. It is what he is made for and where he is going. The only other person in the New Testament called that is Judas (John 17:12), which is its own quiet commentary: the last great enemy and the betrayer share a name, and both of them, for all their apparent power, end where God said they would.

Where Christians differ: who is the man of lawlessness? Interpretations include: a Roman emperor of Paul’s own time; the papacy, as most of the Reformers held (the original Westminster Confession 25.6 named the Pope as antichrist, and the 1689 London Baptist Confession 26.4 does the same); a principle of evil throughout history rather than a person; or a single individual who will appear just before Christ’s return. Verdict: Paul describes a person (“man,” “he”), revealed at a particular time, destroyed at Christ’s coming (v. 8). So the best reading is that he is a final individual, the climactic embodiment of rebellion against God, appearing at the end of the age just before Christ’s return. Yet the mystery of lawlessness is already at work (v. 7), and many antichrists have come (1 John 2:18): throughout history, persons and powers have shown his spirit, including religious systems that claim God’s authority for themselves. The Reformers rightly saw that spirit at work in the abuses of their day. Believers should not speculate about names, but stay faithful and discerning.

A caution about names. Christians have identified this figure with a long series of candidates across twenty centuries, emperors, popes, dictators, and every confident identification so far has been wrong. Nero, Muhammad, Napoleon, Hitler, Stalin: each was named by sincere believers as the man of sin, and each died without being destroyed by the appearing of Christ. That record should make us modest. Paul gives a pattern to recognise, not a name to guess.

Does the great falling away mean true Christians can lose their salvation? No. Those who fall away are those who professed faith without possessing it. John says of such people: they went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2:19). Jesus says his sheep will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of his hand (John 10:28). The apostasy is real and terrible, and it should make every professing believer examine himself (2 Corinthians 13:5); but the elect are kept by God’s power through faith (1 Peter 1:5). Paul will say in v. 13 that these believers were chosen to be saved. The rebellion sifts the church; it does not defeat the Shepherd.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ’s return is delayed indefinitely. These events could unfold quickly, and the spirit behind them is already at work. Paul is not giving them a reason to relax, but a reason not to panic.

In a sentence. Do not let anyone deceive you in any way, for that day will not come until the rebellion occurs and the man of lawlessness is revealed, the man doomed to destruction.

On a Tuesday. Ask yourself what would keep you from falling away if many around you did. Not your upbringing, or your church’s size, or your circle of friends; those are exactly what shift when a great defection comes. Only a real hold on Christ, fed by his word and prayer, will stand. If your faith is mostly borrowed, make it your own now, while the pressure is light.

For worship. Ask God to keep you from deception, and faithful when others fall away, and then rest in the One who keeps. The rebellion is foreknown, the lawless one is named in advance as the son of destruction, and his end is written before his beginning. Christ is not caught off guard by any defection, any deceiver or any dark figure of history. He is the faithful Shepherd who loses none of those the Father gave him, and the King whose day will come exactly when he has said, after everything he has said must come first.

verseByVerse.quote: who opposes and exalts himself against every so-called god or object of worship, so that he takes his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
who opposes and exalts himself against every so-called god or object of worship, so that he takes his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God.

Who opposes and exalts himself against every so-called god or object of worship. The portrait is drawn in two strokes: what he opposes, and what he claims. Not merely against the true God, but against every object of worship. He sets himself against all religion, true and false, and above every object of worship. This is not a rival religion. It is the abolition of religion as such, clearing the field so that nothing is left standing to be worshipped except himself. Paul is drawing on Daniel, and his readers would have heard it: the king who shall exalt himself and magnify himself above every god, and shall speak astonishing things against the God of gods (Daniel 11:36). Daniel’s immediate subject was Antiochus Epiphanes, who in 167 BC set up an altar to Zeus in the Jerusalem temple and offered unclean sacrifices on it, the abomination of desolation. Behind both stands the boast of the king of Babylon: I will ascend to heaven, I will make myself like the Most High (Isaiah 14:13–14). Paul is saying: that pattern again, and worse.

So that he takes his seat in the temple of God. “Temple” (naos) is the inner sanctuary, the holy place itself, not the outer courts. And the seat is the point. He does not merely enter; he sits, which is what one does on a throne or in a place of settled authority.

Proclaiming himself to be God. The ultimate blasphemy, the original sin taken to its extreme. The serpent’s offer was you will be like God (Genesis 3:5). Here is a man who accepts the offer publicly and requires everyone else to agree. And the Thessalonians did not have to imagine it. The Roman emperor Caligula had ordered his own statue set up in the Jerusalem temple in AD 40, about a decade earlier, and the empire came close to a Jewish war over it before he was assassinated. Everyone knew that story. It was a recent memory for Paul’s readers, and it showed them what Daniel meant.

Where Christians differ: which temple? Some take the temple of God to be a rebuilt Jewish temple in Jerusalem, where the antichrist will sit. Others take it as the church, God’s temple in the New Testament (1 Corinthians 3:16; 2 Corinthians 6:16), where false claims to divine authority arise; or as a picture of usurping God’s place. Verdict: Paul uses temple language for the church elsewhere, and the New Testament never predicts a rebuilt temple with divine approval; Christ is the true temple (John 2:19–21). The language most likely draws on Daniel’s imagery to describe the man of lawlessness usurping God’s place and claiming divine honours, perhaps within what claims to be the church. The point is clear whatever the location: he claims to be God. Christians need not look for a rebuilt temple as a sign.

The same material, smaller. What is not in doubt is the character of the thing, and it is the oldest temptation in Scripture wearing its final form. Which means the passage is not only about a figure at the end. Every smaller version of that claim, every self that sets itself above every authority and expects the world to arrange itself around it, is made of the same material. The tyrant who demands worship, the culture that says nothing is above the self, the church leader who will not be questioned, and the ordinary heart that says, in its own small kingdom, my will be done: all of them are rehearsals.

What it does not mean. It does not mean this figure has real divine power. He is a creature, and will be destroyed. He can claim the seat; he cannot make himself God by sitting in it.

Should we expect a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem as a sign of the end? No. If a temple were rebuilt, it would be a matter of politics and history, not a fulfilment of God’s plan, because the New Testament teaches that the sacrifices are finished in Christ (Hebrews 10:11–14, 18) and that God’s temple now is his people, built on Christ the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:19–22). Watching Jerusalem for building work is not what Paul asks of us. Watch instead for the thing he describes: a power that sets itself in God’s place and demands what belongs to God alone, especially when it does so in the name of religion.

In a sentence. He will oppose and will exalt himself over everything that is called God or is worshipped, so that he sets himself up in God’s temple, proclaiming himself to be God.

On a Tuesday. The essence of lawlessness is self-exaltation. Where are you tempted to put yourself in God’s place? Perhaps in insisting that your plans cannot be interrupted, or that your judgement cannot be questioned, or that your feelings decide what is right. Name one area today where you are acting as if you were the final authority, and hand it back to God in prayer.

For worship. There is one who had every right to sit in the temple of God and claim to be God, and he did not grasp at it. Christ Jesus, being in the form of God, emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and humbled himself to the death of the cross (Philippians 2:6–8). The lawless one seizes a throne that is not his; the Son laid aside the glory that was his. And so God has highly exalted him and given him the name above every name, and every knee, including the knee of the man of lawlessness, will bow to him.

parallels.desc: exalt himself and magnify himself above every god

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not remember that when I was still with you I told you these things?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not remember that when I was still with you I told you these things?

Do you not remember that when I was still with you I told you these things? One sentence, and it changes how the whole passage should be read. Paul is not introducing new material. He is reminding them of teaching they had already received in person, and being slightly exasperated that he has to. He had taught them about the end during his short visit. They should have remembered and not been shaken.

One side of a conversation. That explains why the paragraph is so allusive. He writes the rebellion and the man of lawlessness and what is restraining him with definite articles and no explanation, because his readers had heard him spell it out. We are reading one side of a conversation whose other half was spoken aloud in a Macedonian house and never written down. This is the honest reason the restrainer in the next verses is obscure to us and was not obscure to them. You know what is restraining him now: they did; we do not. Any interpreter who claims certainty there is claiming to have recovered a conversation Paul did not record.

Eschatology for new converts. But notice also what it tells us about Paul’s teaching. He was in Thessalonica for perhaps a month, working night and day at a bench (1 Thessalonians 2:9), with brand-new converts out of paganism. In that time he taught them about the apostasy, the man of lawlessness, the restrainer and the sequence of the last things, in enough detail that he can now refer to it in shorthand. Measure that against how we usually pitch teaching for new believers. Paul evidently did not regard eschatology as advanced material to be held back until people were ready. He gave it to a few weeks’ worth of converts, and when they later panicked, the remedy he reached for was: you already know this.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we cannot understand the main point. The main point is clear: the day has not yet come, certain things must happen first, and Christ wins.

If some of Paul’s spoken teaching is lost, are we missing something we need? No. God has given us in Scripture everything necessary for his glory and our salvation, faith and life (Westminster 1.6). What Paul said aloud in Thessalonica on this subject helped them with details we cannot now recover, but nothing we need for faith and obedience was left out of what God caused to be written. The parts of this chapter that are dark to us are dark at the edges, not at the centre. Hold firmly what is clear, hold loosely what is uncertain, and do not let anyone fill the gap with a confident guess.

In a sentence. Don’t you remember that when I was with you I used to tell you these things?

On a Tuesday. What have you been taught that you have forgotten? Paul’s remedy for panic was memory. Go back this week to something you learned well once and have let slip: a passage you studied, a sermon series, a catechism answer. Review it until it is yours again. A believer who remembers what he was taught is very hard to frighten.

For worship. Ask God to help you remember what you have learned from his word, so you are not shaken, and thank him that he does not leave his children to work out the future alone. He tells his people ahead of time. He told the Thessalonians in their first weeks, and he has told us in his written word, because the Lord who holds the end loves to share his counsel with his friends (John 15:15). We are not left guessing in the dark; we are reminded by a Father who has already spoken.

verseByVerse.quote: And you know what is restraining him now so that he may be revealed in his time. For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work. Only he who now restrains it will do so until he is out of the way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you know what is restraining him now so that he may be revealed in his time. For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work. Only he who now restrains it will do so until he is out of the way.

And you know what is restraining him now. These are the two most argued-over verses in the letter, and honesty about what we do not know is the first requirement. Note first a grammatical oddity any theory has to account for. In v. 6 the restrainer is neuter: to katechon, what restrains, the thing. In v. 7 it is masculine: ho katechōn, he who restrains, the person. Something and someone is holding back the man of lawlessness. Paul moves between a force and a person without explanation, because his readers knew what he meant (v. 5) and we do not.

So that he may be revealed in his time. In God’s appointed time, not before. God controls the timetable. The lawless one does not choose his own hour and cannot force it. Even the final rebellion runs on a timetable set by the one it is rebelling against. That is the pastoral point in a passage full of darkness, and it is why Paul can describe all this to a frightened church without leaving them frightened.

For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work. Present tense, in the first century. The principle of rebellion against God is already active, though not yet fully revealed. The thing that will finally appear in one figure is not dormant until then; it is operating now, underground. Mystery here means something hidden and not yet disclosed: the same principle, working in the dark, waiting. Every age has seen it surface, in persecuting emperors, in cruel ideologies, in churches that set men in the place of Christ, and every age has also seen it pushed back down.

Only he who now restrains it will do so until he is out of the way. When the restrainer is removed, the man of lawlessness will appear. What the passage does say plainly, whatever the restrainer is, should be held onto. Evil is currently being held back. There is something at work restraining what would otherwise be unleashed, which means the world as we find it, bad as the news is, is not evil running at full strength. Someone has a hand on it.

Where Christians differ: who is the restrainer? No one now knows for certain what “restrains” the lawless one; the Thessalonians knew (v. 6), but we do not. Suggestions include: the Roman empire and the rule of law (the most common early church view); the Holy Spirit; the preaching of the gospel; the archangel Michael; or Paul himself. Some dispensationalists argue that the restrainer is the Holy Spirit in the church, removed at a pre-tribulation rapture. Verdict: The best answer is humility: Paul does not tell us. Most likely he refers to God’s restraining providence, working through the order of government and law (Romans 13:1–4), which holds back the full outbreak of lawlessness until God permits it. Nothing in the passage teaches a secret rapture of the church; Paul never mentions believers being removed here, and the gathering to Christ comes with his visible coming (v. 1).

Weighing the proposals. Each has real support. The Roman state and the rule of law held anarchy back, and Paul elsewhere calls the governing authority God’s servant (Romans 13:4); this would also explain why he writes so guardedly, since predicting the empire’s removal in writing was dangerous. The preaching of the gospel, which must go to all nations first (Matthew 24:14), is a serious suggestion. The angelic guardian Michael, who stands over God’s people in Daniel (Daniel 12:1), fits the masculine. Paul himself is the weakest candidate, since he died long ago and the restraint continues. And the Holy Spirit, as the restrainer who is removed, faces the problem that the Spirit is everywhere and is never taken from the world. Behind every candidate stands God himself, whose hand holds the restraint and who alone decides when to lift it.

Does until he is out of the way mean the church will be taken away first? Dispensational Christians argue that the restrainer is the Spirit working through the church, so that when the church is raptured, the lawless one will be revealed. But Paul never says the restrainer is the church, the Spirit is everywhere and cannot leave the world, and the next verse says the lawless one is destroyed by the appearance of his coming (v. 8), the same coming at which believers are gathered (v. 1). The church is not the thing removed. It is the people who will see the lawless one appear and then see him fall.

What it does not mean. It does not mean evil is out of God’s control. Even its timing is under him.

If evil is being restrained, why is the world still so bad? Because what we see is sin under restraint, not sin at full strength, and that should frighten and comfort us at once. Every law that punishes violence, every court that convicts a thief, every conscience that flinches, every government that keeps a basic order, is part of God’s restraining mercy (Romans 13:3–4). Without it the world would be unlivable. The evil that breaks through is real and grievous, and God will judge it; but the fact that we can still live, work, marry, worship and raise children is a daily gift of a God who is holding back the flood.

In a sentence. And now you know what is holding him back, so that he may be revealed at the proper time. For the secret power of lawlessness is already at work; but the one who now holds it back will continue to do so till he is taken out of the way.

On a Tuesday. Pray for those in authority this week by name: your national leaders, your local council, the police, the judges (1 Timothy 2:1–2). Their work, however imperfect, is one of the means by which God holds back lawlessness so that the gospel can be preached and his people can live quiet and peaceable lives. And respect the order around you, keeping the law where it does not require sin, because lawlessness in small things belongs to the same mystery.

For worship. Thank God that he restrains evil in the world. Behind every court, every conscience and every quiet street is the hand of the God who said to the sea, thus far shall you come, and no farther (Job 38:11). The mystery of lawlessness works, but only within a fence he has drawn; it will be revealed, but only in his time; and when it is let out at last, it will be let out only to be destroyed. The whole history of evil is a leash in the hand of our Father.
verseByVerse.note: No one now knows for certain what “restrains” the lawless one; suggestions include the rule of law, the Roman empire, and the preaching of the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and bring to nothing by the appearance of his coming.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and bring to nothing by the appearance of his coming.

And then the lawless one will be revealed. After the restrainer is removed. After all that build-up, the apostasy, the self-deifying figure, the restrainer taken away, the mystery of lawlessness working for centuries, here is the confrontation. It is over before it begins.

Whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth. There is no battle. No struggle, no cost, no uncertainty about the result. The Lord does not raise an army or draw a sword; he exhales. The word is pneuma, breath, the same word as spirit and wind. Paul is quoting Isaiah, where the shoot from the stump of Jesse shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall kill the wicked (Isaiah 11:4). John sees the same thing: from the mouth of the rider on the white horse comes a sharp sword, and the enemies of God fall before it (Revelation 19:15, 21). Christ simply speaks, and the lawless one is destroyed. The word that said let there be light, and the word that said Lazarus, come out, is the word that ends him.

And bring to nothing by the appearance of his coming. The second phrase does the same work. “Appearance” is epiphaneia: manifestation, shining forth, the word for a god’s visible appearing; and “coming” is parousia again. He brings him to nothing by the shining-out of his arrival. Not by what he does on arriving. By arriving. The mere brightness of Christ’s arrival ends him. The lawless one is undone the way darkness is undone when somebody opens a shutter, and the man who claimed to be God is undone by the true God’s appearing.

The proportions are the message. That deliberate anticlimax is the passage’s whole pastoral strategy, and it is easy to miss because the earlier verses are so vivid. Paul has spent several verses making this figure as alarming as possible, and then disposes of him in half a sentence, with a breath. Whatever this power turns out to be, it is not in the same category as the one who ends it. That is how the chapter should be read by anyone inclined to be frightened by it. Paul’s aim is not to give the church a monster to watch for. It is to tell a shaken congregation that the worst thing coming will be dealt with by the Lord Jesus without effort, and that their part, as the next verses will say, is to hold on to what they were taught.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the lawless one has real equal power. There is no cosmic contest of two near-equals. His end is certain and swift.

Is this the same as the battle of Armageddon? It describes the same reality: the final overthrow of every power opposed to Christ at his return (Revelation 16:14–16; 19:11–21). But notice how both passages present it. Revelation’s battle has no fighting described; the armies gather and are struck down by the sword from Christ’s mouth. Paul’s version has only a breath. Scripture never pictures the end as a long war whose outcome is in doubt. It pictures a gathering of rebellion and then its instant collapse before the appearing of the King. That one event, the visible coming of Christ, brings the resurrection, the gathering of his people, the destruction of the lawless one and the final judgement together.

In a sentence. And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will overthrow with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the splendour of his coming.

On a Tuesday. No evil power, however great, can stand before Christ. Take courage. Think of the thing in the news or in your own life that most frightens you: a regime, an ideology, a disease, a person who has power over you. Put it in this verse. Whatever it is, it is smaller than the breath of Jesus. Pray about it with that size in mind.

For worship. The Lord Jesus does not need to strain against his enemies. The whole accumulated rebellion of history, given its moment and its champion, does not survive his appearing. One breath, one shining, and it is over. This is the King we serve: the Word through whom the worlds were made, whose speech is power, whose presence is light, and before whose face every claim to deity falls silent. Let the nations rage. He has only to come.

parallels.desc: with the breath of his lips he shall kill the wicked

verseByVerse.quote: The coming of the lawless one is by the activity of Satan with all power and false signs and wonders, and with all wicked deception for those who are perishing, because they refused to love the truth and so be saved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The coming of the lawless one is by the activity of Satan with all power and false signs and wonders, and with all wicked deception for those who are perishing, because they refused to love the truth and so be saved.

The coming of the lawless one is by the activity of Satan. Note the word Paul chooses for his arrival: parousia, the royal-visit word he has used of Christ. The counterfeit runs all the way down, even to the vocabulary. This is a satanic counterfeit of Christ’s return. The lawless one has a coming, a revealing, signs and wonders, and a claim to be God, and behind it all is the activity, the energeia, the working energy, of Satan. Satan energises him. The devil has never created anything; he can only imitate and distort.

With all power and false signs and wonders. Power, signs and wonders: the standard biblical trio for God’s own mighty works. It is how Peter describes the ministry of Jesus at Pentecost, a man attested to you by God with mighty works and wonders and signs (Acts 2:22). The lawless one has the same list, here in counterfeit. And the adjective attached is false: literally, of the lie. Not that the phenomena are necessarily fake conjuring tricks, but that they are lies, signs pointing somewhere untrue. A sign is a pointer, and these point away from God. That should be taken seriously by anyone inclined to treat the miraculous as self-authenticating. Miracles alone do not prove truth. Deuteronomy had already ruled on it: if a prophet gives a sign and it comes to pass, and then says let us go after other gods, do not listen, for the LORD is testing you (Deuteronomy 13:1–3). Jesus said the same, that false christs would perform great signs (Matthew 24:24), and John saw the beast’s prophet make fire come down from heaven (Revelation 13:13–14). The test of a message is never its power. It is its truth.

And with all wicked deception for those who are perishing. Deception is his main weapon. He does not chiefly conquer by force but by persuasion: a lie dressed as light, a miracle in the service of falsehood. And it works on those who are perishing, who are already on the road to ruin.

Because they refused to love the truth and so be saved. Then Paul explains why the deception works, and it is the most searching sentence in the chapter. Read it carefully. He does not say they failed to grasp the truth, or were never given it, or found the arguments unconvincing. He says they refused to love it. The reason they are deceived: they would not love the truth. The problem is located in the affections, not the intellect. Truth was available and they did not want it. That is not merely ignorance but a moral refusal to receive and love the gospel, and it is not curable by better evidence. They are responsible. And notice the little clause hanging on the end: and so be saved. Loving the truth was the road out. It was open. Paul does not present these people as trapped by circumstances beyond them; he presents them as having declined a rescue. That is what makes the next two verses bearable, and it is where they have to be read from.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers will be deceived. Those who love the truth are kept. Jesus said the false signs would lead astray, if possible, even the elect (Matthew 24:24): if possible, which means it is not.

How can I tell a true work of God from a false one? Not by how impressive it is, but by what it points to and whether it agrees with Scripture. Ask: does this exalt the Christ of the Bible, crucified and risen, as Lord? (1 John 4:1–3). Does the message match what the apostles taught, or add to it? (Galatians 1:8). Does it lead people to repentance, holiness and love, or to fascination with the spectacular and with the person doing it? A genuine answer to prayer, a healing, a providence, will always send you to Christ and his word. Anything that makes you need a new revelation, a special leader or a sign to believe is already leading you away.

Can a real Christian be deceived? A believer can be confused, misled for a time, or wrong on many things; the Thessalonians themselves were shaken by a false message. But a true believer will not finally be carried away into the lie of the lawless one, because God keeps his own and gives them a love for the truth that he does not let die (John 10:27–29). The way God keeps us is not by making deception impossible to meet, but by giving us his word, his Spirit and his church, and by making us love the truth. Stay close to all three.

In a sentence. The coming of the lawless one will be in accordance with how Satan works. He will use all sorts of displays of power through signs and wonders that serve the lie, and all the ways that wickedness deceives those who are perishing. They perish because they refused to love the truth and so be saved.

On a Tuesday. Ask God to give you a love for the truth. It is your protection against deception. And notice where truth costs you something: the passage you avoid because it rebukes you, the doctrine you resist because it humbles you, the fact about yourself you would rather not hear. Love for the truth is tested exactly there. Choose the truth today in one place where a comfortable lie would be easier.

For worship. Christ is the truth (John 14:6), and he is not merely a correct idea but a Person to be loved. The devil can counterfeit power and copy signs, but he cannot counterfeit the cross, and he cannot make anyone love the truth. Only God does that. Every heart that has ever turned toward Christ with love has been turned by grace, and that grace is stronger than every lie the father of lies can tell.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore God sends them a strong delusion, so that they may believe what is false, in order that all may be condemned who did not believe the truth but had pleasure in unrighteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore God sends them a strong delusion, so that they may believe what is false, in order that all may be condemned who did not believe the truth but had pleasure in unrighteousness.

Therefore God sends them a strong delusion. This is one of the hardest sentences in Paul, and it should not be softened. God is the subject of the verb. He sends it. “Strong delusion” is energeia planēs: a working of error, an active power of deception. Start with the word therefore, because everything depends on it. This is not God’s opening move. It follows v. 10: because they refused to love the truth. The delusion is a judicial response to a prior refusal, not an arbitrary act on a neutral party. Nobody in this passage wanted the truth and was prevented from having it. Because they refused the truth, God judicially gives them over to their choice. He confirms the blindness they chose.

The old pattern. It runs right through Scripture. It is what happened to Pharaoh, who hardened his own heart, and whose heart God hardened (Exodus 8:15; 9:12). It is the lying spirit God permitted to deceive Ahab’s prophets, after Ahab had spent his life refusing the true word (1 Kings 22:19–23). It is Romans 1, where three times God gave them up to what they had already chosen (Romans 1:24–28). The judgement, in each case, is that God stops obstructing a person’s own direction of travel. He lets them have what they insisted on. There is a terrible mercy in the restraint that precedes it, and a terrible justice in its removal.

So that they may believe what is false. Literally, the lie: the great lie of the lawless one, that he is God. It is the lie of the garden in its final form, and people who would not have the truth are given the lie they preferred.

In order that all may be condemned who did not believe the truth but had pleasure in unrighteousness. Verse 12 states the outcome and repeats the ground, and the pairing is exact. They did not merely disbelieve; they enjoyed the alternative. The root issue: they delighted in sin, so they rejected truth. Paul consistently traces unbelief to what a person loves. Unbelief is often moral before it is intellectual: the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil (John 3:19–20).

Where Christians differ: does God cause people to believe lies? Some find this incompatible with God’s goodness. Verdict: God is not the author of sin, and he does not deceive the innocent. He sends delusion as a judgement on those who have already refused the truth and loved unrighteousness, giving them over to what they chose. Like the hardening of Pharaoh, it confirms and punishes persistent rebellion (Westminster 5.6). The sinner remains fully responsible.

What it does not mean. It does not mean anyone who wants the truth is prevented from finding it. Those who seek find (Matthew 7:7).

Could this describe me? I am afraid I am deluded. Anyone anxious that this describes them has, by that anxiety, given the evidence against it. The mark of the people in these verses is that they do not want the truth and are content. Wanting it is the opposite condition, and it is the beginning of the road out that v. 10 says was open. This passage has never been given to anyone as a diagnosis of their neighbours, nor as a weapon for tender consciences. It was written to comfort a church that was wondering how so many could be taken in, and the answer is that God is not absent even from that, and the outcome is not in doubt. If you want Christ, come to him; he has promised never to cast out anyone who comes (John 6:37).

In a sentence. For this reason God sends them a powerful delusion so that they will believe the lie, and so that all will be condemned who have not believed the truth but have delighted in wickedness.

On a Tuesday. Do not toy with sin. Loving unrighteousness leads to blindness. The process is gradual: a sin enjoyed, then excused, then defended, then a doctrine adjusted to make room for it. Notice if you have begun reading the Bible to find permission rather than direction. If there is a sin you are enjoying, bring it into the light today, before your mind starts building arguments for it. Love the truth.

For worship. God is just in every judgement, and nothing he sends is unfair. But the same God who gives the persistent rebel over to the lie he chose has, for countless others, refused to give them over. He pursued us when we too loved the darkness, broke through our preferences, and gave us a love for the truth we did not have. That we see at all is mercy. That we love Christ at all is grace. The difference between the deluded and the saved is not that we were wiser, but that he was kind.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: By contrast Paul thanks God for the Thessalonians, loved by the Lord, because God chose them for salvation through the Spirit’s sanctifying work and their belief in the truth, calling them through the gospel to share Christ’s glory. So they must stand firm and hold on to the teaching they received, by word or letter. Paul prays that the Lord Jesus and God the Father, who loved them and gave them eternal comfort and good hope by grace, will encourage their hearts and strengthen them in every good deed and word.
verseByVerse.theology:
Election, and the Means It Arrives By

Verse 13 compresses the whole of salvation into one Trinitarian sentence — God chose, the Spirit sanctified, they believed, and glory lies ahead — and verse 14 refuses to let election float free of the means: it reached them ‘through our gospel’.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: After the lawless one and the delusion, what Paul asks for is undramatic: stand firm and hold to what you were taught.

Now: A congregation that knows what it was given is very hard to panic — and what eschatology is for is steadiness in ‘every good work and word’ (v.17).

verseByVerse.quote: But we ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers beloved by the Lord, because God chose you as the firstfruits to be saved, through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth. To this he called you through our gospel, so that you may obtain the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But we ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers beloved by the Lord, because God chose you as the firstfruits to be saved, through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth. To this he called you through our gospel, so that you may obtain the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.

But we ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers beloved by the Lord. One of the great reversals in Paul. He has just described people who refused the truth, were given over to a delusion, and stand condemned. Then he turns to the congregation and the contrast is total, point for point: not perishing, but beloved. They refused to love the truth; these were chosen. They were given a delusion; these were sanctified by the Spirit. They had pleasure in unrighteousness; these believed the truth. Paul is not changing the subject; he is showing them the other side of the same coin, and it is deliberate comfort for people who had just been badly frightened. And the address: brothers beloved by the Lord. In the first letter he called them loved by God (1 Thessalonians 1:4); here the love is Christ’s. It is a small shift and a large claim, made without any argument at all.

Because God chose you as the firstfruits to be saved. Here is the compressed statement of salvation, and it is Trinitarian in one sentence: God chose you, through sanctification by the Spirit, so that you may obtain the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ. Father, Spirit, Son: choosing, sanctifying, and the glory they are travelling toward. “Chose you as the firstfruits” involves a genuine textual question. The Greek manuscripts divide between aparchēn, firstfruits, and ap’ archēs, from the beginning, and the two look almost identical in the uncial script. Some manuscripts read chose you from the beginning, as the ESV notes: from eternity. Firstfruits would mean among the first converts in Macedonia, the first sheaf of a harvest God would go on reaping. Either way, election: the initiative was God’s and it came first. The difference does not affect the doctrine.

Through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth. The means: the Spirit sets them apart, and they believe the truth. God chose the end (salvation) and the means (the Spirit’s work and faith). Unlike those who refused to love the truth, these believed it.

To this he called you through our gospel. Then v. 14 anchors it to something they can remember. Election was worked out in history through the preaching of the gospel and the effectual call. The eternal choice reached them through three men preaching in their town. Paul never lets election float free of the means: it arrived by way of a sermon somebody actually delivered, which is exactly the point he made at 1:10 about the testimony that was believed.

So that you may obtain the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ. The goal: sharing Christ’s glory. The golden chain again: chosen, called, sanctified, believing, glorified (Romans 8:30). And set it beside v. 4, where the lawless one grabs at the place of God. These people will receive glory as a gift. The thing the usurper tries to seize is given away freely to a persecuted congregation in Macedonia.

What kind of election is this? Arminian Christians hold that God chose those he foresaw would believe. But Paul says God chose them to be saved, through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth: faith and holiness are the means God chose to bring them to salvation, not the reason he chose them. The cause of the choice lies in God, in his love, not in anything foreseen in them.

How can I know I am chosen? Not by looking into God’s secret decree, but by what God has done. Look at the chain Paul gives: called through the gospel, believing the truth, being made holy by the Spirit. If you have believed the truth and the Spirit is making you holy, you have the marks of God’s choice. You do not climb into heaven to read the book of life; you look at Christ, trust him, and see the fruit he is producing. Election is not a riddle to be solved before you dare to believe. It is a comfort given to those who already believe, to tell them their faith was God’s idea before it was theirs.

If God has chosen, why should we evangelise? Because God chose the means as well as the end. He chose these people to be saved through belief in the truth, and he called them through our gospel. No one believes without hearing, and no one hears without a preacher (Romans 10:14). Election is the reason evangelism succeeds, not the reason to stop. Paul endured everything for the sake of the elect, that they might obtain salvation (2 Timothy 2:10). We do not know who they are; we preach to everyone, and God brings his own.

What it does not mean. It does not mean election makes faith unnecessary. God chose them to be saved through belief.

In a sentence. But we ought always to thank God for you, brothers and sisters loved by the Lord, because God chose you as firstfruits to be saved through the sanctifying work of the Spirit and through belief in the truth. He called you to this through our gospel, that you might share in the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.

On a Tuesday. When the news is full of lawlessness and you wonder whether the church will survive, read these two verses aloud. Then thank God by name for three believers you know, as Paul did, tracing his work in each: chosen, called, believing, being made holy. And if you are unsure of your own standing, do not search your feelings; look at the gospel, believe it again, and ask the Spirit to make you holy.

For worship. Thank God that he chose you, called you through the gospel, and destined you for glory. Before you had done anything, before you existed, the Father set his love on you; at the right moment the gospel found you; the Spirit is even now making you holy; and the glory of Christ is waiting at the end of the road. Not one link in the chain was forged by you, and not one can be broken by the lawless one or the devil behind him. Glory belongs to the God who chooses, calls, keeps and crowns.

verseByVerse.quote: So then, brothers, stand firm and hold to the traditions that you were taught by us, either by our spoken word or by our letter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So then, brothers, stand firm and hold to the traditions that you were taught by us, either by our spoken word or by our letter.

So then, brothers, stand firm. After the apostasy, the man of lawlessness, the restrainer, the delusion and the condemnation, this is what Paul actually asks them to do. Two verbs, and neither is dramatic. Because God chose and called you, do not be shaken. “Stand firm” is stēkete, the soldier holding his position, the same word Paul used in the first letter (1 Thessalonians 3:8). Not advance, not counter-attack, not work out the timetable. Hold the ground you are on.

And hold to the traditions that you were taught by us. “Hold” is krateite: grip, keep hold of. And paradoseis, traditions, means simply what has been handed over: a deposit passed from one person to the next. Here it means the apostolic teaching handed on to them, not later church customs. Paul uses the same family of words for what he received about the Lord’s Supper and the resurrection and then delivered on (1 Corinthians 11:23; 15:3). It is not human custom accumulating over time; it is apostolic teaching in transit.

Either by our spoken word or by our letter. Paul’s oral teaching while present, and his letters. Paul puts his preaching and his writing on the same level and gives them equal authority. What he said in their house and what he sent by courier are the same deposit in two forms. That is a significant sentence, and it is early: one of the first indications anywhere that apostolic writing was regarded as carrying the weight of apostolic speech. The spoken half we no longer have, as v. 5 has already reminded us. The written half is what we are reading.

Where Christians differ: Scripture and tradition. The Roman Catholic Church cites this verse to argue that there are two sources of authority: Scripture and unwritten apostolic tradition passed down through the church. Orthodox churches hold a similar view. Verdict: Paul’s oral and written teaching had equal authority, because both came from the apostle. But the content of the apostolic tradition is now preserved for us in the written Scriptures. We have no reliable access to other apostolic oral teaching beyond what is written. The apostles’ spoken teaching was the same gospel they wrote down, and Paul himself points the church to what we say in this letter (3:14). So Scripture alone is now the final and sufficient rule of faith, by which all later traditions must be tested (Westminster 1.6, 10; 2 Timothy 3:16–17).

The answer to the crisis. See how directly this answers the chapter’s emergency. They had been shaken by a spirit, a word, or a letter claiming to be his (v. 2). The remedy is not a new revelation to settle the matter, and not a better prophet. It is: go back to what you were actually taught, and hold on. A congregation that knows what it was given is very hard to panic.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all tradition is bad. Creeds and confessions are valuable when they faithfully summarise Scripture. The Apostles’ Creed, the Nicene Creed, and the great Reformation confessions are handed-on treasure, and wise Christians read them gladly. But they stand under Scripture, and are to be corrected by it.

What does holding to the traditions look like in practice? It means knowing what the apostles taught well enough to recognise when someone departs from it. Read the New Testament regularly and whole, not only in fragments. Learn a good summary of the faith, a catechism or confession, so that the shape of the gospel is fixed in your mind. Sit under preaching that explains the text. And when a new teaching arrives, however exciting or however authoritative the speaker, ask where it is written. Holding on is not a feeling of conviction; it is a habit of returning, again and again, to the word that was handed to you.

In a sentence. So then, brothers and sisters, stand firm and hold fast to the teachings we passed on to you, whether by word of mouth or by letter.

On a Tuesday. Hold fast to the apostolic teaching in Scripture. Let it steady you when others are shaken. Choose one New Testament letter and read it through in a sitting this week, as its first hearers did. You will find that the traditions Paul meant are not hidden or complicated. They are the gospel, set down for you in writing.

For worship. The Lord of the church has not left his people to the winds of every new voice. He spoke through his apostles, and he caused what they taught to be written, preserved, and placed in our hands, so that a believer in any century can hold the same deposit the Thessalonians held. His word is a rock under shaking feet. Blessed be the God who speaks, and who keeps his word for his people to stand on.
verseByVerse.note: “Traditions” here means the apostolic teaching handed on to them, whether in person or in writing.

verseByVerse.quote: Now may our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us and gave us eternal comfort and good hope through grace, comfort your hearts and establish them in every good work and word.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now may our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us and gave us eternal comfort and good hope through grace, comfort your hearts and establish them in every good work and word.

Now may our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father. The chapter that has contained the darkest material in the letter ends in prayer, and the grammar is the same quiet marvel as in the first letter. Christ is named first here, then the Father: an equal place. Paul is not observing any protocol of rank, and it would be an odd thing to write if he thought the two were on different sides of the line between Creator and creature. And the verbs that follow (comfort, establish) are singular, as in 1 Thessalonians 3:11: two subjects, one action. The Father and the Son act as one. Paul names the Son and the Father and speaks of them acting together without explanation; it is not a doctrine being argued but the ordinary shape of his praying.

Who loved us and gave us eternal comfort and good hope through grace. Three things said about God, all in the past tense, before anything is asked. Past tense: a decisive act of love, at the cross. The request in v. 17 rests entirely on what has already been done. Paul does not ask God to start loving them or to begin providing; he asks him to continue in a direction already established. “Eternal comfort” is a striking pairing: encouragement that never runs out. Their comfort in the present had been badly shaken; that is the whole occasion of the letter. Paul tells them the comfort they have been given is of a kind that outlasts the thing shaking it. And good hope is not a wish but a sure expectation of glory, an expectation with grounds; the adjective distinguishes it from the hopeful thinking people fall back on when they have nothing else. All through grace.

Comfort your hearts. They had been shaken (v. 2). May God steady them. The word comfort here (parakaleō) carries the sense of coming alongside to strengthen, not merely to soothe.

And establish them in every good work and word. “Establish” (stērizō) means strengthen, make firm, the buttressing word, to prop what is leaning. It is the very thing Timothy had been sent to do in the first letter (1 Thessalonians 3:2). In deeds and words: a whole life of faithfulness. And note where it lands: established in every good work and word. Not in correct opinions about the end times, which is what the chapter has been about. In what they do and what they say. Paul has just spent twelve verses on the man of lawlessness, and the outcome he prays for is a congregation whose deeds and speech are steady. That is a fair measure of what the doctrine of the last things is for.

What it does not mean. It does not mean comfort comes from knowing every detail of the future. It comes from God’s love and grace.

What if I do not feel comforted? Paul’s prayer assumes the comfort has already been given (gave us eternal comfort) and asks that it would reach their hearts. The gift and the feeling of it are not the same. Your comfort rests on facts: God loved you, Christ died for you, your hope is secured by grace. Feelings follow facts slowly, and sometimes only after a long night. So do what Paul did: pray for it. Ask the Father and the Son to comfort your heart, rehearse what they have done, and keep doing the next good work and speaking the next good word while you wait. The steadiness often comes in the doing.

In a sentence. May our Lord Jesus Christ himself and God our Father, who loved us and by his grace gave us eternal encouragement and good hope, encourage your hearts and strengthen you in every good deed and word.

On a Tuesday. Pray this blessing for someone who is anxious about the future: a teenager frightened by the news, an older believer facing death, a friend shaken by a loud prophecy. Pray it over them by name, and then send them a message with these two verses in it.

For worship. The Lord Jesus Christ himself and God our Father loved us, and that love is already history; it happened, at a cross outside Jerusalem, and nothing in the future can make it not have happened. From that love flows a comfort with no end date and a hope with solid ground beneath it, all of grace. The Father and the Son, acting as one, hold up what is leaning and steady what is shaken, and they will go on doing it until the day the Son appears and every fear is answered with his face.
