3.title: The Lord Is Faithful
3.overview:
Paul asks for prayer that the word of the Lord will run ahead, and assures them that the Lord is faithful and will guard them. Then he deals firmly with a problem that has grown since his first letter: some believers, probably excited about Christ’s return, have stopped working and are living off others while meddling in everyone’s business. Paul had worked night and day to support himself as an example, and had taught them, “If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat.”

The church must withdraw ordinary support and fellowship from such people, so that they are brought to their senses, yet treat them as brothers, not enemies. Those who have carried the load must not grow weary of doing good. The letter ends with peace, Paul’s own signature against forgery, and grace for all.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul asks them to pray that the Lord’s message will spread and be honoured as it was with them, and that the missionaries will be rescued from wicked people, since not everyone has faith. But the Lord is faithful; he will strengthen and protect them from the evil one. Paul is confident they are doing what he commands, and prays that the Lord will direct their hearts into God’s love and Christ’s endurance.
verseByVerse.theology:
Faithless, and Faithful

‘Not all have faith’ — ‘but the Lord is faithful’ (vv.2–3): Paul answers human faithlessness not with a better estimate of people but with a reliable Lord, who promises not exemption from trouble but to establish and guard his people through it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul wrote from Corinth, where Acts 18 records exactly the ‘wicked and evil men’ of verse 2.

Now: Confidence placed ‘in the Lord about you’ (v.4) survives disappointment, because it never rested on the people themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, brothers, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may speed ahead and be honored, as happened among you, and that we may be delivered from wicked and evil men. For not all have faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finally, brothers, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may speed ahead and be honored, as happened among you, and that we may be delivered from wicked and evil men. For not all have faith.

Meaning first. 2 Thessalonians 3 turns from the great events of the end (chapter 2) to the ordinary life of a church waiting for them. It falls into three parts. First, prayer and confidence (vv. 1–5): Paul asks the church to pray that the gospel will run freely and that he will be rescued from hostile men; he assures them that the Lord is faithful and will guard them from the evil one; and he prays that the Lord will direct their hearts into God’s love and Christ’s steadfastness. Second, a problem of discipline (vv. 6–15): some members had stopped working, perhaps excited by talk of the Lord’s return, and were living off others and meddling in their affairs. Paul commands the church to keep away from them, points to his own example of working night and day, repeats the rule he gave when he was with them (whoever will not work should not eat), orders the idle to work quietly and earn their own living, and tells the church to shun the disobedient, not as enemies but as brothers who need warning. Third, the close (vv. 16–18): a prayer for the Lord of peace to give them peace, Paul’s signature in his own hand as a mark against forgeries, and the blessing of grace. The chapter shows that a right hope of Christ’s coming does not make people idle; it makes them faithful, busy and orderly. The same Lord who will come in flaming fire is the Lord who guards a small church through an ordinary week, and both are the same faithfulness.

The setting. In 1 Thessalonians Paul had already told the church to work with their hands and live quietly (1 Thessalonians 4:11–12) and to warn the idle (1 Thessalonians 5:14). The problem had grown. The false report that the day of the Lord had already come (2:2) may have fed it: if the end is here, why go on working? Or the idle may simply have been taking advantage of the generosity of richer believers, as clients in Greek cities lived off patrons. Either way, Paul treats it as a matter of obedience to the apostolic tradition, not merely of manners.

Finally, brothers, pray for us. “Finally” (to loipon, as for the rest) marks the move to the closing section, not the very last word. “Pray” is present tense: keep praying. The apostle who has just written about the man of lawlessness and the strong delusion turns to a harassed provincial congregation and asks them to pray for him. The apostle who prays for them (1:11) asks them to pray for him. He does it in letter after letter, and it never becomes a formality. Prayer runs both ways in the body of Christ; no minister is above needing the prayers of his people.

That the word of the Lord may speed ahead. And notice what he asks for. Not safety, not release, not success, but the progress of the message. “Speed ahead” (trechē) is literally run, and Paul is almost certainly hearing Psalm 147:15, where God’s word runs swiftly. The picture is of a runner carrying a message, or of a herald who cannot be overtaken, racing forward without obstruction. He asks for the message to move, not for the messenger to be comfortable. And the word is of the Lord: it is Christ’s word, carried by Paul.

And be honored, as happened among you. “Be honoured” (doxazētai) means be glorified: the same thing he prayed for in 1:12. The word is glorified when people receive it as God’s word and their lives are changed by it, rather than merely hearing and shelving it. Then the gracious clause: as happened among you. He holds up their own conversion as the pattern of what he is asking God to do elsewhere (1 Thessalonians 1:5–6; 2:13). These people were currently frightened, confused about the last things, and harbouring a group who had stopped working. Paul tells them they are his example of the gospel running well. At this time he was in Corinth, and he wanted Corinth to become what Thessalonica had become.

And that we may be delivered from wicked and evil men. The second request is more personal. “Delivered” (rhysthōmen) means rescued. “Wicked” (atopos) is literally out of place: perverse, unreasonable, people with whom argument does not work. “Evil” (ponēros) is actively malicious. The definite article in Greek (the wicked and evil men) suggests particular opponents, probably those in Corinth who opposed Paul. Acts 18 records exactly this: a united attack, Paul dragged before the proconsul Gallio (Acts 18:5–17). He is not speaking in generalities. The gospel advances in the face of opposition, and Paul asks for prayer for protection so that the work can continue.

For not all have faith. Literally, for not of all is the faith. A short sentence with a good deal of weight in it, reading almost as an understatement, and it is Paul’s explanation for opposition. He does not attribute hostility to misunderstanding, or assume better presentation would resolve it. Some people do not believe, and their not believing has consequences for those who do. This is a sober realism: not everyone believes, and some who reject the gospel actively fight it. Unbelief is the root of opposition to the gospel. It also prepares for v. 3 by contrast: people are unfaithful, but the Lord is faithful.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the progress of the gospel depends finally on our prayers rather than on God. God has ordained that his purposes advance through the prayers of his people; prayer is a real means he uses, not a lever that overrules him. Nor does “not all have faith” mean that faith is something all people could produce if only they tried harder; faith is God’s gift (Ephesians 2:8; Philippians 1:29), which is why Paul prays.

If God is sovereign, does my prayer actually change anything? Yes, because God has chosen to work through it. He decreed not only the ends but the means, and the prayers of his people are among the means (James 5:16). Paul did not think the gospel would run whether or not the Thessalonians prayed; he asked them because he believed their prayers would be part of how God made it run. Sovereignty is not a reason to stop praying; it is the reason prayer is worth anything. You are not asking a God who might be unable, but a God who is able and who delights to answer.

When I meet hostility for sharing my faith, have I done it wrong? Not necessarily. Paul met it constantly, and he was not tactless; he simply said, for not all have faith. Sometimes we do handle things badly, and we should be humble enough to ask (Colossians 4:5–6; 1 Peter 3:15–16). But the gospel itself offends, and the most gracious witness in history was crucified. Knowing this in advance prevents a Christian from concluding, every time he meets real opposition, that he must have failed. Be gentle, be clear, and leave the result with God.

In a sentence. Last of all, keep praying for us: that the Lord’s message will race on and be honoured everywhere as it was with you, and that we will be rescued from perverse and malicious men, because faith is not something everyone has.

On a Tuesday. Pray this week for one missionary or minister by name: that the word would run through their work, and that they would be protected from those who oppose it. Ask them what to pray for, and then tell them you did. And pray for your own minister before Sunday, not only after it.

For worship. The word of the Lord runs. It ran out of Jerusalem to Samaria, to Antioch, across the sea to Macedonia, through a prison in Philippi and a riot in Thessalonica, and it has never been overtaken. Kings have tried to chain it and it has run past them. The Lord Jesus sends his word swiftly over the earth, and where it lands and is received it is glorified, because it is his own voice raising the dead. That it reached us is the proof that it cannot be stopped.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Lord is faithful. He will establish you and guard you against the evil one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the Lord is faithful. He will establish you and guard you against the evil one.

But the Lord is faithful. Read it directly after v. 2 and you will hear the wordplay: not all have faith (pistis), but faithful (pistos) is the Lord. The same root, twice, set against each other. Human faithlessness is real and Paul has just named it; the sentence that answers it is not about better people but about a reliable Lord. The word faithful stands first in the Greek sentence for emphasis. “The Lord” here is Christ, as throughout these letters. His faithfulness means he keeps his promises and finishes what he begins: he who calls you is faithful, and he will surely do it (1 Thessalonians 5:24; 1 Corinthians 1:9; Philippians 1:6).

He will establish you. “Establish” (stērixei) means make firm, set fast, strengthen: the buttressing word, to prop what is leaning. It is the fourth time it has appeared in the Thessalonian correspondence: Timothy was sent to establish them (1 Thessalonians 3:2), Paul prayed God would establish their hearts (1 Thessalonians 3:13; 2 Thessalonians 2:17), and now he states it as a promise. These were people who had been shaken (2:2), and the promise is aimed exactly at that. Paul turns quickly from his own danger to theirs. They were under persecution; the Lord himself would hold them up.

And guard you against the evil one. “Guard” (phylaxei) is a sentry’s word: to keep watch over, protect, like a garrison, a picture close to Philippians 4:7. “The evil one” (tou ponērou) could grammatically mean evil in general, but here, after chapter 2’s talk of Satan’s activity (2:9), it almost certainly means Satan himself, as in the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:13) and Jesus’ prayer for his disciples (John 17:15). It is the petition of the Lord’s Prayer, answered as a statement. Satan wants to shake believers loose, by persecution, by false teaching, or by disorder in the church. Christ guards his own.

In it with them. Notice the direction of the whole verse. Paul has asked them to pray for him because of dangerous men, and then immediately assures them that the Lord will guard them. He asks for prayer and gives reassurance in the same breath, which is the mark of someone who is genuinely in it with the people he is writing to rather than above them. And there is a quiet realism here worth naming. Paul does not promise they will be spared trouble; he has just spent a chapter and a half saying they will not be. He promises they will be held and guarded through it. That is a different assurance, and it is the only one Scripture ever actually gives.

Where Christians differ: can a true believer finally fall away? Arminian and some Lutheran traditions teach that a genuine believer may lose salvation by turning away. Verdict: Verses like this one ground the Reformed doctrine of perseverance. The promise rests not on our grip on Christ but on his faithfulness: “he will establish you and guard you.” Those whom God has chosen and called (2:13–14) he keeps to the end (John 10:28–29; Romans 8:30; 1 Peter 1:5). This does not make warnings pointless; the warnings are among the means by which he keeps us. And those who finally fall away show that they were never truly his (1 John 2:19).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers will never be attacked or never stumble. Satan does attack, and believers do sin. It means the Lord will not let the evil one finally destroy their faith. Nor does it make us passive: Paul still commands them (v. 4) and prays for them (v. 5).

What does an attack of the evil one look like in an ordinary Christian life? Rarely anything dramatic. More often it is an accusation that will not let you rest in forgiveness (Revelation 12:10), a doubt pressed at a weak moment, a temptation timed to your tiredness, a quarrel stirred in the church, or a lie about God’s goodness whispered in suffering. Scripture tells us to resist him, firm in the faith (1 Peter 5:8–9), and to put on the armour God supplies: truth, righteousness, the gospel, faith, the word, and prayer (Ephesians 6:10–18). You do not fight alone. The Lord who guards you has already defeated him at the cross (Colossians 2:15).

In a sentence. People may be faithless, but the Lord is utterly faithful: he will make you stand firm and keep you safe from Satan.

On a Tuesday. Think of the point at which you feel most likely to give way: a habit, a fear, a relationship, a doubt. Bring that exact point to Christ in prayer and ask him to set a guard there. Then say v. 3 aloud. Your security is not your watchfulness, though you must watch; it is his.

For worship. When you feel your own grip on faith is weak, rest on his faithfulness. Thank him that your safety depends on his keeping, not on your strength. People fail, churches fail, and our own hearts fail us daily, but the Lord is faithful. He has never once let go of anyone the Father gave him. He stands sentry over his people in the dark, he holds up what is leaning, and the evil one, for all his rage, cannot pluck a single one of them out of his hand.

verseByVerse.quote: And we have confidence in the Lord about you, that you are doing and will do the things that we command. May the Lord direct your hearts to the love of God and to the steadfastness of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we have confidence in the Lord about you, that you are doing and will do the things that we command. May the Lord direct your hearts to the love of God and to the steadfastness of Christ.

And we have confidence in the Lord about you. “Have confidence” (pepoithamen, perfect tense) means we have been persuaded and remain so: we trust. Paul is about to issue some hard instructions, and he prepares the ground by expressing confidence first. Anyone who has to correct somebody should copy it. This is a pastoral move before the hard command of v. 6: he expresses trust before giving correction. But look where the confidence is placed: in the Lord about you. Not in their natural goodness or their track record, which had already wobbled. Because the Lord is at work in them (v. 3), Paul can trust that they will obey. That is a form of confidence that survives disappointment, because it was never resting on the person in the first place.

That you are doing and will do the things that we command. “Command” (parangellō) means give orders, charge: a military and legal word. It appears four times in this chapter (vv. 4, 6, 10, 12). Paul speaks with apostolic authority: his instructions are not suggestions but the Lord’s commands through his apostle (1 Thessalonians 4:2). The church is already obeying and will go on obeying.

May the Lord direct your hearts. Then a short prayer, and both halves repay attention. “Direct” (kateuthynai) means make straight, guide straight along a path, clear a road. It is the same verb he used in 1 Thessalonians 3:11, asking God to clear the way to Thessalonica. There it was a journey; here it is the heart. The affections need a road made through them as much as a traveller does. Obedience is not merely outward; it begins in the heart, and only the Lord can steer the heart: the king’s heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD (Proverbs 21:1).

To the love of God. Grammatically this could be our love for God or God’s love for us. Most likely Paul means God’s love for us: may the Lord lead you deeper into the experience and knowledge of God’s love (Romans 5:5; Ephesians 3:19), from which our love for God flows. Both are true, and the first produces the second. You learn to love God by being brought into his love for you.

And to the steadfastness of Christ. “Steadfastness” (hypomonē) is patient endurance, bearing up under a load. Again it could be Christ’s own endurance, which they are to see and share (Hebrews 12:2–3), or the endurance that Christ gives and that waits for him. Probably both: the patient endurance that Christ showed under suffering, which he now works in his people as they wait for his return. This is the right response to chapter 2: not feverish excitement, but steady endurance. And the phrase is the striking one for this congregation. They needed staying power, and Paul does not tell them to find more of it. He asks God to point their hearts at Christ’s own endurance, at a man who kept going all the way to a Roman cross. Steadfastness is not manufactured by resolution. It is drawn from somebody who has already done it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s authority was his own. He commands “in the Lord.” Nor does it mean obedience is earned salvation; it is the fruit of hearts that the Lord has directed into his love.

How does the Lord direct my heart into his love in practice? Usually through ordinary means, used slowly. He sets his love before you in his word, especially at the cross (Romans 5:8; 1 John 4:10). He pours it into your heart by the Spirit (Romans 5:5). He shows it in the Lord’s Supper, in the fellowship of his people, and in providences you can trace afterwards. So put yourself where the road is being cleared: read of his love, meditate on it, sing it, and pray this verse. When your heart drifts toward fear, resentment or self-pity, ask him to turn it back, and then look again at Christ.

In a sentence. Because the Lord is at work in you, we are sure you are doing, and will keep doing, what we instruct; may he steer your hearts deep into God’s love and into the steady endurance that Christ showed and gives.

On a Tuesday. Before you correct anyone this week, a child, a colleague, a fellow believer, first tell them honestly what you are confident of in them, and where that confidence rests. Then speak. And when you are tired of enduring, do not grit your teeth harder; spend five minutes reading of Christ’s endurance in the Gospels and ask him to share it with you.

For worship. Pray this for yourself today: Lord, steer my heart into your love, and give me the endurance of Christ. The love of God is not a feeling we must work up but an ocean we are led into, and the endurance of Christ is not a standard we must reach but a strength he shares. He endured the cross, despising the shame, for the joy set before him, and he is now steering the hearts of his people home along the road he cleared.

verseByVerse.ref: 3:6–15 – Idleness, and How to Deal With It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul commands them, in the Lord’s name, to keep away from any believer who lives in idleness, refusing to work. The missionaries themselves set the example: they did not eat anyone’s food without paying, but worked hard night and day so as not to burden anyone, not because they had no right to support, but to give a model to copy. Their rule was that anyone unwilling to work should not eat. Some are idle busybodies; they must settle down and earn their own living. The others must not grow tired of doing good. Anyone who ignores this letter is to be noted and avoided, so that he is ashamed, yet treated as a brother to be warned, not as an enemy.
verseByVerse.theology:
Discipline That Aims at Restoration

Verses 14 and 15 must be held together: the withdrawal is real, and its aim is the offender's own recovery; and he is still to be warned as a brother. Drop the firmness and the church helps nobody; drop the warmth and discipline becomes expulsion.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul could command the idle to work only because he had worked night and day in front of them, declining support he had every right to (vv.7–9).

Now: Verse 10 is about the unwilling, not the unable, and it governs the church's own table. And verse 13 speaks to the faithful who have carried more than their share: do not stop.

verseByVerse.quote: Now we command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you keep away from any brother who is walking in idleness and not in accord with the tradition that you received from us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now we command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you keep away from any brother who is walking in idleness and not in accord with the tradition that you received from us.

Now we command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. The tone changes sharply. In the first letter Paul asked and urged (1 Thessalonians 4:1); here he commands, and does it under the highest authority available. Something has hardened since he last wrote. This is the fullest and most solemn form of authority Paul could use: not his own name, but Christ’s. “In the name of” means by his authority and as his representative. What follows is not advice but a binding instruction for the church.

That you keep away from any brother. “Keep away” (stellesthai) means draw back, hold aloof, withdraw from. The word was used of furling sails, shortening sail, or keeping one’s distance. It is not excommunication: v. 15 will forbid treating the man as an enemy and insist he is still a brother to be warned. The person is still called a brother: this is discipline inside the family of faith, not a declaration that he is an unbeliever. What is being withdrawn is the ordinary support and easy fellowship that had been enabling the behaviour. If the community keeps feeding a man who will not work, the community is paying him to stay as he is. The point is to stop treating him as though nothing were wrong, so that he feels the weight of the church’s disapproval.

Who is walking in idleness. “In idleness” (ataktōs) means disorderly, out of line. The word was used of soldiers breaking ranks, out of formation, and in everyday papyri of apprentices skipping work; it is the word of 1 Thessalonians 5:14. In context (vv. 7–12) the specific disorder is refusing to work and living off others. “Walking” is the Bible’s word for a settled way of life, not a single slip. This is not about outsiders or about the poor. It is about members of the congregation who had stopped working.

And not in accord with the tradition that you received from us. “Tradition” (paradosis, what is handed down) is the same word as in 2:15. The apostolic tradition included not only doctrine but how to live, including the duty to work (1 Thessalonians 4:11–12). This tradition is now found in the New Testament, the written form of what the apostles handed down. The problem is not that these people are irritating but that they are contradicting apostolic teaching by how they live. Paul treats a lifestyle as capable of being out of accord with the deposit, exactly as a doctrine can be.

Setting and background. Why might some have stopped working? Three main suggestions: (1) eschatological excitement, believing the day had come (2:2) and that work was pointless; (2) a culture of patronage, in which poorer people attached themselves to wealthier ones and lived on handouts, now transferred to generous church members; (3) a misunderstanding of Christian love, assuming the church owed them support. Paul’s answer covers all three: work is part of faithful waiting, love does not mean being a burden, and the church must not enable idleness.

Where Christians differ: how should church discipline be practised? Some churches practise almost no formal discipline; others make it harsh and quick. Verdict: Scripture requires real discipline, carried out by the church under its elders, aimed at restoring the sinner (Matthew 18:15–17; 1 Corinthians 5; Galatians 6:1). This passage describes a step short of full exclusion: the person is still a brother (v. 15), but the church withdraws close fellowship to bring him to shame and repentance. Discipline is graded to the offence and persistence, and it is always done in love, never as revenge.

Costly, not bureaucratic. It should be said plainly that this is a hard instruction, given to a small congregation where everyone knew everyone. Paul is not writing about institutional procedure. He is telling people to change how they behave toward someone they will see next week, which is far more costly than any formal process, and is the only reason it could work.

What it does not mean. It does not mean shunning those who cannot work because of illness, disability, age, or lack of jobs. The issue is those who will not work (v. 10). Scripture repeatedly commands care for the genuinely needy (Galatians 2:10; 1 Timothy 5:3–16). Nor does it mean cutting off all contact; v. 15 says to warn him, which requires speaking.

What if the person living off others is my own adult child? The principle still applies, with the tenderness of a parent. Love wants the child to flourish, and flourishing includes the dignity of responsibility. Continuing to fund a settled refusal to work, when they are able, is not kindness; it is paying them to stay where they are. That does not mean throwing them out overnight or withdrawing love. It means talking honestly, setting clear expectations and a reasonable timeline, helping them toward work, and being willing to let them feel the consequences of refusing. If there is illness, depression or addiction behind it, get help for that; it is a different situation. Pray, keep speaking, and keep the door of the heart open.

In a sentence. By the authority of the Lord Jesus Christ we instruct you to hold yourselves apart from any fellow believer who has broken ranks and lives in idleness, contrary to the teaching we handed on to you.

On a Tuesday. Ask honestly: does your church’s kindness ever enable someone’s settled refusal to take responsibility? Loving them may mean refusing to go along with it. And ask the same of yourself: is there a responsibility God has given you that you have left others to carry?

For worship. The Lord Jesus Christ governs his church, and he does it as its Head and its Shepherd. His name is not a weapon to beat the wayward but the authority of the one who loves them enough to stop them. He never broke rank with his Father’s will. He worked the works of the one who sent him while it was day (John 9:4), and he finished the work he was given (John 17:4). The church that bears his name is called to walk in step with him, and when one of its members falls out of line, the whole body is called to go after him in Christ’s name, for his good.
verseByVerse.note: The problem of idleness in the church is now worse than when Paul wrote the first letter.

verseByVerse.quote: For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us, because we were not idle when we were with you, nor did we eat anyone's bread without paying for it, but with toil and labor we worked night and day, that we might not be a burden to any of you. It was not because we do not have that right, but to give you in ourselves an example to imitate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us, because we were not idle when we were with you, nor did we eat anyone’s bread without paying for it, but with toil and labor we worked night and day, that we might not be a burden to any of you. It was not because we do not have that right, but to give you in ourselves an example to imitate.

For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us. Before pressing the command, Paul points at himself. “Imitate” (mimeisthai) means follow as an example; our word mimic comes from it. Paul often calls believers to follow his example as he follows Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1; Philippians 3:17; 1 Thessalonians 1:6). Doctrine was taught by word and shown by life. “You ought” (dei, it is necessary): this imitation is a duty.

Because we were not idle when we were with you. “Were not idle” (ouk ētaktēsamen, we did not break ranks) is the verb form of the word in v. 6. Paul and his companions did not behave in the disorderly way some were now behaving.

Nor did we eat anyone’s bread without paying for it. The detail is specific enough to be checked. “Eat bread” is a Hebrew way of saying get one’s living (Genesis 3:19; Amos 7:12). “Without paying” (dōrean) means as a gift, free. Paul did not live on anyone’s charity while in Thessalonica, though the Philippians sent him gifts there more than once (Philippians 4:16).

But with toil and labor we worked night and day. It is almost word for word what he wrote in the first letter (1 Thessalonians 2:9): the leatherworker’s bench, the double shift, the refusal to be carried. Two words are stacked again for the work: “toil” (kopos), wearying work, labour to exhaustion, and “labour” (mochthos), hardship, hard struggle, the grind. Paul is not describing a trade he enjoyed but being tired. He was a tentmaker (Acts 18:3), working with leather, and he worked long hours, probably starting before dawn, while also preaching and teaching.

That we might not be a burden to any of you. “Be a burden” (epibarēsai) means weigh down. Paul did not want his support to fall on a young, poor and persecuted church, and he did not want anyone to say he preached for money (1 Thessalonians 2:5–6; 2 Corinthians 11:7–9).

It was not because we do not have that right. This is the sentence that keeps the passage from becoming a rule about ministers never being paid. “Right” (exousia) is authority, entitlement. He had the right. Paul firmly taught that those who preach the gospel have the right to be supported by it: the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:4–14; Galatians 6:6; 1 Timothy 5:17–18; Luke 10:7). He gave up this right voluntarily, here, for a specific reason.

But to give you in ourselves an example to imitate. That reason is stated exactly. “Example” (typos) is a pattern, model, the impression left by a stamp or die: the same word he used of the Thessalonians themselves (1 Thessalonians 1:7). Paul deliberately made himself a living pattern of honest work, working harder than he needed to and going without money he was entitled to, in order to leave a shape these people could copy, so that no one could excuse idleness by appeal to spirituality. If the apostle himself worked, so could they. And that is what makes the command of v. 6 possible at all. Paul is not a man asking a congregation to do something he has arranged to be exempt from. He had sat at a bench in their town before dawn and after dark. When he tells the idle to work, every person reading the letter knows he has already done it in front of them, and that is the only footing from which anyone has ever successfully told anyone else to change.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ministers should never be paid. Paul defends the right of ministers to support elsewhere, and Scripture commands it. It means ministers may sometimes waive that right for the sake of the gospel, and that all believers, including ministers, should model diligence. Nor does it mean manual work is less spiritual than preaching; Paul did both, and both were service to Christ.

Is my ordinary job really service to Christ? Yes, if it is lawful work done in faith. Paul’s leatherwork was part of his ministry, not a distraction from it, because it adorned the gospel and served his neighbours. The Reformers recovered this: the farmer, the nurse, the mother, the accountant, the cleaner all have a calling from God, not merely the minister. Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, for you are serving the Lord Christ (Colossians 3:23–24). Your diligence, honesty and cheerfulness at work are worship, and they preach to colleagues who will never enter a church.

In a sentence. You know well that you should follow our pattern: we did not break ranks while we were with you or live on anyone’s handouts, but worked hard and long, day and night, so as not to weigh on any of you; we had every right to support, but we gave it up to make ourselves a model for you to copy.

On a Tuesday. Do your work today as part of your witness. Someone is watching how a Christian works: whether you arrive on time, whether you finish what you start, whether you complain, whether you cut corners when no one checks. And if you lead others, in a family, a team or a church, ask whether you are asking them to do anything you are not doing yourself.

For worship. The Son of God spent most of his earthly life at a carpenter’s bench in Nazareth, and those hidden years were as pleasing to his Father as the miracles. He did not count work beneath him. He laid aside his rights, as Paul did after him, and became the pattern stamped on all his people: he came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). Every honest day’s work done in his name bears the impression of his hands.

verseByVerse.quote: For even when we were with you, we would give you this command: If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For even when we were with you, we would give you this command: If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat.

For even when we were with you, we would give you this command. “We would give” is the imperfect tense: we kept giving it, repeatedly. He kept saying it. This was not a new rule invented for the crisis but part of Paul’s basic instruction to new converts, standing instruction from the beginning. Teaching about work was part of discipleship from the beginning. It belongs with the pattern of vv. 7–9: he had told them and he had shown them.

If anyone is not willing to work. It is among the best-known sentences Paul wrote and among the most abused, so the qualification in the middle of it has to be seen. The key word is “willing” (thelei, wants, chooses). The rule targets those who refuse to work, not those who are unable. Paul is dealing with a choice of the will, not with misfortune. This is not about anyone who cannot find work, cannot do work, or cannot get enough of it. It is about the settled refusal to work by someone who is able. Paul is addressing people who had chosen idleness, perhaps for what they took to be spiritual reasons, and who were eating at the expense of a poor congregation while they did it.

Let him not eat. A command (third-person imperative), not merely a prediction. The church was not to feed those who could work but would not. Similar sayings existed in Jewish wisdom (Proverbs 10:4; 19:15; 20:4), and the principle reaches back to creation: humanity was made to work (Genesis 2:15), and after the fall work became toil but remained a calling (Genesis 3:19). God himself worked six days and rested; work is part of the image of a working God.

Not a verse against the poor. That distinction is not a modern softening; it is what the verse says, and everything else in Paul confirms it. This is the man who organised a major international collection for the poor of Jerusalem across several years and several letters (Romans 15:25–27; 2 Corinthians 8–9), who was eager to remember the poor (Galatians 2:10), who told the Galatians to do good to everyone (Galatians 6:10), and who wrote that anyone who does not provide for his household has denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8). A verse used to justify indifference to the poor is being used against its author. Two things make the rule humane rather than harsh. It is aimed at the will, not at capacity. And it is a rule for the community’s table: Paul is telling the church what to do with its own resources. Refusing to subsidise a choice is a different act from abandoning a person, and v. 15 will make sure nobody confuses them. Underneath it is the same principle as 1 Thessalonians 4:11–12: idleness here is a failure of love, because the idle man’s food comes from somewhere, and the somewhere is his brothers. The command is not an attack on the poor. It is a defence of them.

Setting and background. Early churches shared meals and supported the needy generously (Acts 2:44–45; 4:34–35). That generosity could be exploited. This rule protects the church’s charity for those who truly need it, and protects the idle from the harm of being enabled.

What it does not mean. It does not mean refusing help to the sick, disabled, elderly, unemployed through no fault of their own, or those caring for others. Nor does it mean that a person’s worth depends on productivity; every human bears God’s image. It also does not by itself settle every question of public welfare policy; Paul is speaking to the church about its own members. What it does mean is that able people who refuse to work should not expect others to support them, and that true love sometimes says no.

How do I apply this when someone asks me for money? Begin with generosity, not suspicion: give to the one who begs from you (Matthew 5:42) is still Christ’s word. But generosity can be wise. Where you can, give in ways that meet real needs, food, a bill paid directly, help finding work, rather than cash that may feed an addiction. Within the church, let the deacons or leaders who know the situation guide the help, so that the genuinely needy are cared for generously and the able but unwilling are lovingly pressed to work. When in doubt, err on the side of mercy, and ask God for wisdom (James 1:5).

In a sentence. Even while we were among you we kept giving this rule: whoever refuses to work should not be fed.

On a Tuesday. Work is a gift and a calling from God, not just a way to pay the bills. Do today’s work as to the Lord (Colossians 3:23). If you are tempted to coast, remember that someone, somewhere, is carrying what you put down.

For worship. My Father is working until now, and I am working, said Jesus (John 5:17). The God of the Bible is not idle. He upholds the universe by the word of his power, feeds the birds, clothes the lilies, and sustains every breath of every creature. He made us in his image to work as he works, and in Christ he restores that dignity to the weary and the broken. Even our labour is grace: the strength to do it, the bread that comes from it, and the rest that waits at the end of it are all from his hand.

verseByVerse.quote: For we hear that some among you walk in idleness, not busy at work, but busybodies. Now such persons we command and encourage in the Lord Jesus Christ to do their work quietly and to earn their own living.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we hear that some among you walk in idleness, not busy at work, but busybodies. Now such persons we command and encourage in the Lord Jesus Christ to do their work quietly and to earn their own living.

For we hear that some among you walk in idleness. Paul had received a report, perhaps from the bearer of the first letter. “Some” (tinas): not the whole church, but a group. “Walk in idleness” (peripatountas ataktōs) is the same word as v. 6: living a disorderly life.

Not busy at work, but busybodies. The English catches a pun that is in the Greek too: mēden ergazomenous alla periergazomenous, not working, but working around. Not busy, but busy in others’ business. Doing no business, but minding everyone else’s. The wordplay is not decoration; it is the diagnosis. Idleness is never actually idle. The energy does not disappear when a person stops working; it gets redirected, and it goes into other people’s affairs: spreading gossip, interfering, perhaps stirring up excitement about the end. A man with nothing to do and opinions about everyone is a recognisable figure in any congregation, and Paul had one or two of them in Thessalonica. Idleness and meddling go together (1 Timothy 5:13). That is also why this is a church problem and not a private one. Someone who has stopped working is not merely failing to contribute; he has time on his hands in a small community, and the meddling that follows does real damage. The first letter had already told them to mind their own affairs (1 Thessalonians 4:11). The advice had not taken.

Now such persons we command and encourage in the Lord Jesus Christ. Paul speaks directly to the idle. Note both verbs. “Command” (parangellō): this is not a suggestion. And “encourage” (parakaleō): urge, exhort, appeal, the coming-alongside word. Firm authority with a warm appeal. He does not choose between firmness and warmth. The people who need telling are also being urged, not simply ordered. “In the Lord Jesus Christ”: both the authority and the motive are Christ. Paul does not write them off; he calls them back.

To do their work quietly. “Quietly” (meta hēsychias) means with quietness, calmness: the opposite of the restless, meddling busyness of v. 11. It echoes 1 Thessalonians 4:11: aspire to live quietly, mind your own affairs, and work with your hands. Quietness here is not silence but a settled, undisturbed way of life. And what he asks for is unremarkable. There is a deliberate contrast with the busybodies. The cure for meddling is not a rule against gossip; it is a job.

And to earn their own living. Literally, that they eat their own bread: bread they have earned, not bread given by others. It is a direct echo of v. 8, where Paul did not eat anyone’s bread without paying. He is asking them to do exactly what he did in front of them. The instruction is not a burden he has designed for other people. Self-support is a mark of Christian maturity, and it frees the person to be generous to others: let him labour, doing honest work with his own hands, so that he may have something to share with anyone in need (Ephesians 4:28).

What it does not mean. It does not mean every Christian must be in paid employment. Homemaking, caring for family, study and volunteer service are real work. The issue is refusing responsibility and living off others while meddling in their affairs.

Is retirement unbiblical? Not if it is a change of work rather than an end to usefulness. Scripture nowhere commands paid employment to the end of life, and age and weakness are real. But it gives no picture of a long life of self-pleasing leisure either. Retirement can free a believer for prayer, for grandchildren, for serving the church, for hospitality, for mentoring younger Christians, for volunteer work in the community (Titus 2:3–5; Psalm 92:14). The question is not whether you draw a salary, but whether your time is given to God and others or simply spent on yourself.

In a sentence. We are told that some of you are living disorderly lives, not doing any work but busy poking into other people’s business; to such people we give this instruction and appeal, in the Lord Jesus Christ: settle down, get on with your work, and eat bread you have earned.

On a Tuesday. If you find yourself with energy for others’ business, ask whether your own work is done. Quiet faithfulness is a powerful witness. Before you pass on the next piece of news about someone, ask: is this mine to tell, and have I finished what God gave me to do today?

For worship. The Lord Jesus never meddled and never idled. He knew his Father’s business from the age of twelve (Luke 2:49), and he did it with a quietness that the crowds mistook for weakness: he will not quarrel or cry aloud (Matthew 12:19). He did not rush and he did not loiter, and he finished everything his Father gave him. In him the restless are given rest, the meddlers are given a work of their own, and the disorderly are put back in step with heaven.
verseByVerse.note: A wordplay in Greek: not busy at work (ergazomenous) but busybodies (periergazomenous).

verseByVerse.quote: As for you, brothers, do not grow weary in doing good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for you, brothers, do not grow weary in doing good.

As for you, brothers. “As for you” (hymeis de, but you) turns from the idle to the rest of the church, the faithful majority who were working and perhaps supporting the idle. And this one sentence shows how well Paul understood a congregation.

Do not grow weary in doing good. “Grow weary” (enkakēsēte) means lose heart, become discouraged, give up from exhaustion. “Doing good” (kalopoiountes) is a single compound word: doing what is fine, noble, right. Because there is a second casualty in this situation, and it is not the busybodies. It is the people who have been working all along, paying their own way, quietly carrying more than their share, and watching others eat at the common table without contributing. That is genuinely wearying, and Paul names it. And the temptation it describes is precise: when disorder is tolerated, the orderly begin to wonder why they bother. The steady giver notices who is not giving. The reliable one starts to feel like a fool. That corrosion does more long-term damage to a church than the original idleness did, because it works on the people holding everything up. The faithful might be tempted to grow cynical: having been taken advantage of, they might stop helping anyone. Paul says: do not let the misuse of your generosity by a few make you stop doing good to all. Keep working, keep giving to the truly needy, keep acting rightly.

A hand on the shoulder. Notice too what Paul does not do here. He does not tell the faithful to police the others, or to keep accounts, or to withdraw their own good work until the situation is sorted. He has given the community its instruction about the idle in v. 6; to everyone else he simply says: keep going. “Doing good” is broader than the immediate issue; the phrase covers the whole of generous, useful Christian living. So the verse reaches past Thessalonica to anyone who has been faithful for a long time without much to show for it, and who has begun to calculate. Paul’s word to them is not an argument. It is a hand on the shoulder: do not stop. The same exhortation appears in Galatians 6:9, with the promise that in due season we will reap, if we do not give up.

What it does not mean. It does not contradict v. 10. Refusing to enable idleness is itself doing good. The point is that the church should not swing from naive generosity to cold suspicion.

I am exhausted from serving. Does this mean I can never rest? No. Growing weary in doing good means losing heart and giving up, not needing sleep or a holiday. God built rest into creation, and Jesus took his tired disciples away to rest a while (Mark 6:31). Sometimes the faithful thing is to step back from a role for a season, to share the load, or to say no to a new request. What Paul warns against is the bitterness that says: no one appreciates this, so I will stop caring. Rest your body; guard your heart. And remember that the harvest is promised, even when you cannot see it yet.

In a sentence. But you, brothers and sisters, must not lose heart or tire of doing what is right.

On a Tuesday. Has disappointment made you stop helping people? Ask God for wisdom to help well and for grace not to grow weary. Think of one good thing you used to do and quietly stopped doing because someone took advantage, or because no one noticed. Ask whether God wants you to begin again, more wisely.

For worship. The Lord Jesus never grew weary of doing good. He healed lepers who never came back to thank him, fed crowds who wanted only bread, washed the feet of the man who would betray him, and prayed for the soldiers driving the nails. His goodness was not withdrawn when it was abused. That is the goodness that has been poured on us, who also took more than we gave, and it is the goodness that will not stop until it has brought us home. He sees every unthanked kindness done in his name, and none of it will lose its reward.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone does not obey what we say in this letter, take note of that person, and have nothing to do with him, that he may be ashamed. Do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone does not obey what we say in this letter, take note of that person, and have nothing to do with him, that he may be ashamed. Do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother.

If anyone does not obey what we say in this letter. Here is the procedure, and both halves must be held together or the thing becomes either useless or cruel. “What we say in this letter”: Paul’s written word carries the same authority as his spoken word (2:15). Refusing it is refusing apostolic authority. This bears on how we treat the New Testament today: it is the apostles’ word to the church, and it binds us.

Take note of that person. “Take note” (sēmeiousthe) means mark, signal, identify. The church is to recognise openly who is persisting in disobedience, rather than letting everyone gossip about it privately. Not gossip, but a recognised step of church discipline.

And have nothing to do with him. “Have nothing to do with” (mē synanamignysthai) means do not mix together with, do not associate closely. It is the same rare word as 1 Corinthians 5:9, 11, and the same withdrawal as v. 6: the removal of the ordinary fellowship and support that had made the behaviour sustainable. It likely means withdrawing table fellowship and close social intimacy, possibly including the Lord’s Supper, so that the person feels the break.

That he may be ashamed. “Be ashamed” (entrapē) means literally to turn in on oneself, be made to reflect, feel shame. Shame is not a popular category now, and we should be clear what Paul means. He is not after humiliation for its own sake. The word describes the state of a man who is brought up short and suddenly sees how his behaviour looks. In a community where a person genuinely belongs, that recognition is a mercy, because it is the thing that changes him. The aim is repentance: shame that leads him to see his sin and return. The purpose is stated as an outcome for him, not as protection for everyone else.

Do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother. Then the guard, and it is essential. “Warn” (noutheteite) means admonish, literally put in mind, counsel: the word from 1 Thessalonians 5:12, correction aimed at change, not at punishment. He is still a brother. The church does not hate him, curse him or treat him as an outsider. It continues to speak to him, lovingly and seriously, calling him back. Discipline is family correction, not the expulsion of an enemy. So the withdrawal is real and it is limited. The community stops subsidising and stops pretending nothing is wrong; it does not stop speaking to him, and it does not reclassify him as an opponent. Everything in the procedure is designed to get him back.

Where Christians differ: is this the same as excommunication? Some see this as full exclusion from the church; others as a lesser stage. Verdict: This seems to be a step short of full excommunication. In Matthew 18:17 and 1 Corinthians 5:5, 13, the unrepentant is put outside and treated as an unbeliever. Here the offender is still to be warned “as a brother.” Discipline has stages: private warning, warning with witnesses, the church’s withdrawal of close fellowship, and, if repentance never comes, removal from membership. At every stage the goal is restoration (2 Corinthians 2:6–8; Galatians 6:1).

The narrow line. A church that cannot hold both halves will fail in one of two directions, and both are common. Drop the firmness and you get a congregation that tolerates anything and therefore helps nobody: the person is left exactly as he is, which is not kindness. Drop the warmth and discipline becomes expulsion: an enemy made, a person written off, and no road home. Paul walks the narrow line between them in two sentences.

What it does not mean. It does not license harshness, public shaming for entertainment, or cutting off all contact. Paul explicitly forbids treating him as an enemy. Nor does it mean individuals should begin discipline on their own; it is the church’s act, led by its elders.

What do I do if someone under church discipline is my friend? Stay a friend in the way Paul describes: not by pretending nothing has happened, and not by taking his side against the church, but by being one of the voices that calls him back. Do not gossip about the matter, and do not join in easy socialising that tells him all is well. Do speak to him, pray for him, and tell him plainly that you want him restored. If you think the church has acted wrongly, raise it with the elders, not with him. And be ready to be the first to welcome him when he repents (2 Corinthians 2:7–8).

In a sentence. If anyone refuses to follow what we have written in this letter, mark him out and keep away from close company with him, so that he is brought to shame and reflection; yet do not treat him as an enemy, but keep admonishing him as a brother.

On a Tuesday. If you must correct a fellow believer, do it as family: seriously, but with love and hope of restoration. Before you speak, settle in your heart that you want him back more than you want to be proved right. And if you are the one being corrected, receive it as a brother’s warning, not an enemy’s attack.

For worship. Our Lord is the Shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to go after the one, and the Father who runs down the road to the son who is coming home. His discipline is never the cold door of an enemy; it is the firm hand of a family that will not let a brother walk off a cliff. He disciplines those he loves (Hebrews 12:6), and every withdrawal his church makes in his name is meant to end in a feast. There is always a road home, because he made one at the cross.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul prays that the Lord of peace will give them peace at all times and in every way, and be with them all. He adds a greeting in his own handwriting, the mark of every genuine letter from him, and closes with the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord of Peace, and a Signature Against Forgery

Only here does Paul write ‘the Lord of peace’, saying of Christ what a Jew would say of God; and his handwritten signature (v.17) answers the forged letter of 2:2 with a test the church can actually use.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: To a year-old, harassed congregation Paul wrote of flaming fire and the son of destruction, and signed off with grace.

Now: ‘All’, twice in three verses (vv.16, 18), puts even the disciplined inside the blessing — the difference between discipline and rejection.

verseByVerse.quote: Now may the Lord of peace himself give you peace at all times in every way. The Lord be with you all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now may the Lord of peace himself give you peace at all times in every way. The Lord be with you all.

Now may the Lord of peace himself. Elsewhere Paul writes the God of peace (1 Thessalonians 5:23; Romans 15:33). Here, uniquely in his letters, it is the Lord of peace, and Lord throughout these letters means Jesus: Christ, who is the source and giver of peace (John 14:27; Ephesians 2:14). It is another of the quiet, unargued places where Paul says something about Christ that a Jew would only say about God, a quiet sign of his deity. “Himself” is emphatic, as it was at 2:16 and in the great prayer of 1 Thessalonians 3:11. It stresses that peace comes directly from him, not from circumstances. Not an agent, not a process, not a technique for calming down. The Lord himself gives it, which means peace here is not a state they must achieve but a gift that has to be handed over.

Give you peace at all times in every way. “Peace” (eirēnē, Hebrew shalom) is not only calm feelings, but wholeness, well-being, and right relationship with God and one another. Then two phrases that leave nothing out. At all times: in every circumstance, constantly, no moment excluded, including the ones in which the trouble is at its worst. And in every way: in every form, no kind of circumstance excluded, and the word can also mean by every means: however it has to be delivered, let it come. Some manuscripts read in every place. Consider where this sits. This church had persecution from outside (1:4), a forged letter, false teaching about the end (2:2), the man of lawlessness, a strong delusion, and disorder within (3:6–12), with an instruction to withdraw from members of their own church. That is the situation into which Paul prays for peace at all times in every way. Christ’s peace reaches into all of it. He is not describing the absence of trouble; there is no prospect of that. He is asking for something to be given in the middle of it.

The Lord be with you all. The oldest and simplest benediction there is. The greatest blessing is the Lord’s presence: I am with you always, to the end of the age (Matthew 28:20). And note the last word. You all: which in this congregation must include the idle brothers of v. 6 and whoever was to be marked in v. 14. Paul has just told the church to withdraw from them, and he will not close the letter without including them in the blessing. That is the difference between discipline and rejection, said in one word.

What it does not mean. It does not promise an absence of trouble. Peace is given in the midst of trouble (John 16:33; Philippians 4:7).

How do I actually receive this peace? By receiving the Lord who gives it. Peace is not a technique but a Person: he himself is our peace (Ephesians 2:14). Begin with the peace with God that comes through faith in Christ (Romans 5:1), which no circumstance can disturb. Then bring each anxiety to him in prayer with thanksgiving, and his peace will guard your heart (Philippians 4:6–7). Fix your mind on what is true about him (Isaiah 26:3). And do not wait for the trouble to end before expecting peace; Paul prayed for it at all times, which includes now.

In a sentence. May the Lord who is peace himself give you his peace always and in every circumstance; the Lord be with every one of you.

On a Tuesday. Name the specific trouble that is most unsettling you today. Pray v. 16 over it word for word, putting the trouble where the words at all times in every way stand. Then do the next ordinary duty in front of you, trusting that the Lord of peace is with you in it.

For worship. Ask the Lord of peace for his peace in the specific trouble you face today, and rest in his presence. He made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20), and he gives it as no one else can, not as the world gives. He calmed the storm with a word and slept through it first. He walked into a locked room full of frightened men and said, peace be with you, and showed them his hands. That same Lord is with you all, the faithful and the faltering, and his peace is not a mood that comes and goes but the gift of his own presence, which never leaves.

verseByVerse.quote: I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. This is the sign of genuineness in every letter of mine; it is the way I write.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. This is the sign of genuineness in every letter of mine; it is the way I write.

I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. The letter has been dictated to a secretary, and here Paul takes the pen. The handwriting changes on the page. Paul normally dictated his letters to a secretary (an amanuensis; compare Romans 16:22, where Tertius names himself) and then took the pen for the last lines (1 Corinthians 16:21; Galatians 6:11; Colossians 4:18). His handwriting was evidently distinctive: see with what large letters I am writing to you with my own hand (Galatians 6:11).

This is the sign of genuineness in every letter of mine. “Sign” (sēmeion) means mark, token. This time there is a reason beyond affection, and the letter has been building to it. Go back to 2:2, where the trouble started: they had been shaken by a letter seeming to be from us. Somebody had used Paul’s name to unsettle this church. Paul emphasises the signature here because a letter falsely claiming to be from him had confused the church about the day of the Lord. His handwritten signature lets them tell his true letters from forgeries: every genuine letter carries his own hand at the close. “In every letter” implies Paul had already written others, or intended this as his regular practice, and that the church would keep and compare his letters. There is a striking assumption buried in it. Paul is writing very early, and he already expects that there will be more letters, that they will circulate, and that people will need to distinguish the genuine from the false. He is aware that his correspondence carries weight worth counterfeiting.

It is the way I write. Literally, thus I write. His own hand is the guarantee. It is a small, practical, almost bureaucratic solution to a real pastoral problem, and it tells you something about how Paul worked. He answers a forged letter not only with argument, which he has already given them in chapter 2, but with a procedure they can actually use next time. Pastors who have only theology and no practical remedies leave their people defenceless in the interval. And set it beside what this letter has said about holding to the traditions taught either by spoken word or by letter (2:15). The written half of that deposit had to be protected, and here is Paul protecting it in the only way available to him: with his own hand at the bottom of the page.

Textual note. Some critical scholars argue that 2 Thessalonians was not written by Paul, partly because of its strong stress on authenticity, claiming a forger would protest too much. But the stress fits the situation exactly: a forged letter had already caused trouble (2:2). The early church received the letter as Paul’s without dispute; it is listed in Marcion’s canon and the Muratorian Fragment, and cited by Polycarp and Irenaeus. There is no good reason to doubt it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only the signed lines are inspired. The whole letter carries Paul’s apostolic authority; the signature authenticates all of it.

How do we know the books in our Bible are genuine and not forgeries? The same way the Thessalonians did, extended over time. The early churches received the apostles’ letters directly, kept them, copied them and compared them, and they rejected writings that falsely claimed apostolic authority. The books of the New Testament were recognised, not invented, by the church: they carried apostolic origin, agreed with the apostolic gospel, and were received from the beginning by the churches. Above all, God’s word bears its own marks, and the Spirit persuades his people that it is his voice (Westminster 1.5; John 10:27). The canon is closed: no new writing can join it, and none needs to.

In a sentence. I, Paul, add this greeting in my own handwriting; it is the mark that proves every letter of mine is genuine, and this is how I sign.

On a Tuesday. God cared that his people could tell true teaching from false. Test what you hear against the genuine apostolic word, the Scriptures. When a book, a video or a preacher claims to tell you something new from God, ask the Thessalonian question: where is the apostle’s signature on this? If it is not in Scripture, it does not bind your conscience.

For worship. God has not left his people at the mercy of forgers. He who once guided an apostle’s pen to the bottom of a page has watched over his word through every century, so that what we hold is what he gave. The Lord Jesus knows his own voice, and his sheep know it too; the counterfeits come and go, but the word of our God stands forever (Isaiah 40:8). Every page we open is signed, in the end, by the hand of the God who cannot lie.
verseByVerse.note: Paul dictated his letters, then signed off in his own hand — a safeguard against forgeries such as the one hinted at in 2:2.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all.

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. “Grace” (charis) is undeserved favour and its gifts. Paul began with grace (1:2) and ends with grace, as he framed the first letter. It opened with grace to them from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ; it closes with grace be with them. Everything in between, comfort in persecution, hope of glory, the panic about the day of the Lord, the man of lawlessness, the busybodies, correction of error, discipline, rests on grace and sits inside those two sentences, and is answered by what they name. It is the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: it comes to us from him and through him, the crucified and risen Lord.

Be with you all. The same as 1 Thessalonians 5:28, but with all added, as in v. 16. It is the second time in three verses that Paul has reached for that word, and in this congregation it is doing deliberate work. After the stern words of vv. 6–15, Paul pointedly includes everyone. He has just instructed them to withdraw from certain brothers and to mark anyone who disobeys. The final sentence of the letter puts every one of those people inside the blessing. Grace is for the whole church, including the disorderly, whom grace alone can restore.

The note it ends on. That is the right note. Nothing in these three chapters, not the flaming fire, not the eternal ruin, not the withdrawal of fellowship, has been written out of hostility toward anybody. It has been written to hold a church together under pressure and to get its wandering members back. Remember what this congregation was: a few dozen former pagans and synagogue attenders in a proud Roman city, perhaps a year old, harassed by their neighbours, confused about the future, quarrelling about who should be working. Paul had spent only weeks with them. To such people he wrote about flaming fire and the son of destruction and the glory of the Lord Jesus, and then signed off with the only thing that was going to get them through the week. Grace, to the whole lot of them. It is where Paul always ends, because it is the one provision that does not run out.

What it does not mean. It does not mean grace ignores sin. The same letter disciplines sin. Grace both forgives and transforms: the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation, training us to renounce ungodliness (Titus 2:11–12).

In a sentence. May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest on every one of you.

On a Tuesday. End the day where Paul ended the letter. Whatever went wrong, whatever you failed to do, whatever you still fear about tomorrow, place it inside the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and pray that same grace, by name, over the person in your church you find hardest to love.

For worship. End today by thanking Christ for his grace: it began your Christian life, it carries you now, and it will bring you home. Grace found the Thessalonians in their idols and grace kept them under persecution; grace answered their panic, corrected their disorder and promised them glory. The same grace of our Lord Jesus Christ stands at the beginning and the end of every believer’s story, and in between, at every step, it has never once run dry. To him who gives it freely, and who will come again to complete it, be glory for ever.
